scheduling/obstetrics-gynecology.metaTitle: OB/GYN Scheduling Software for Prenatal Care
scheduling/obstetrics-gynecology.metaDescription: OB/GYN scheduling that books the whole prenatal series, pairs ultrasounds with provider visits and keeps procedure slots open. See it on your templates.
scheduling/obstetrics-gynecology.h1: OB/GYN Scheduling Software Built Around the Prenatal Calendar
scheduling/obstetrics-gynecology.subtitle: clinIQ books prenatal visits by gestational week, pairs ultrasound and lab appointments with provider time, and protects slots for gynecology procedures and urgent pregnancy concerns.
scheduling/obstetrics-gynecology.problemStatement: An OB/GYN schedule mixes two very different practices. Obstetric patients follow a calendar set by gestational age: visits every four weeks early on, every two weeks in the third trimester, then weekly near term, with the anatomy ultrasound and glucose screening landing in narrow windows. Gynecology adds annual exams, colposcopy, IUD insertions and endometrial biopsies that need a procedure room and an assistant. Add on-call physicians pulled to labor and delivery, and a generic slot grid cannot keep up.
scheduling/obstetrics-gynecology.solutionHeading: Templates That Know Prenatal and Procedure Timing
scheduling/obstetrics-gynecology.solutionStatement: clinIQ sizes each visit type to its real length and requirements. A new OB intake gets a long block with the nurse. A routine return visit gets a short one. Colposcopy and IUD templates reserve the procedure room and the assistant. Schedulers book a pregnancy's visits as a series tied to the due date, so key screenings land inside their windows. When a physician is called to labor and delivery, staff see which patients to move and which can stay with another provider.

workflow.h2: How a Pregnancy Moves Through clinIQ Scheduling
workflow.intro: From the confirmation visit to the postpartum check, the schedule follows the pregnancy instead of the front desk's memory.

steps.title: New OB intake
steps.body: The scheduler selects the new OB template. clinIQ blocks a longer visit with the nurse for history, education and labs, then the provider visit. The estimated due date anchors every later appointment, so staff never count weeks by hand on a paper wheel or a desk calendar.

steps.title: Series booked by week
steps.body: Return visits book out on the standard cadence for the patient's gestational age. The anatomy ultrasound and glucose screening are paired with a provider visit on the same day where the rooms allow it. Patients leave knowing their next several dates instead of calling back each month.

steps.title: Changes absorbed
steps.body: If a high-risk patient needs added visits or testing, staff add them to the series without rebuilding it. When a patient cancels, the [waitlist](/features/scheduling) offers the slot by text to another patient whose visit window fits, and a yes reply books it without a phone call.

steps.title: Postpartum and back to gynecology
steps.body: After delivery, the postpartum visit is booked on its own template with the time it needs for recovery, feeding and mood screening, and contraception planning. The patient then moves into annual well-woman scheduling, so the relationship continues past the pregnancy and routine gynecology care stays with the practice.

items.title: Procedure room rules
items.body: Colposcopy, LEEP, IUD insertion and endometrial biopsy templates reserve the procedure room, the equipment and a medical assistant. Two procedures cannot be booked into the same room at the same time.

items.title: Provider type matching
items.body: Templates specify who can see each visit: physicians, certified nurse midwives or nurse practitioners. Routine prenatal returns can go to any qualified provider with open time, while new consults and high-risk follow-ups stay with physicians.

items.title: On-call disruption handling
items.body: When a physician leaves for a delivery, the provider view shows the rest of the affected session. Staff move short return visits to a colleague with open time and contact the remaining patients before they leave home.

items.title: Protected urgent slots
items.body: Same-day capacity for bleeding, decreased fetal movement or pain concerns is held and released on rules, so urgent pregnancy calls get seen in the office instead of being sent elsewhere.

items.title: Visit length feedback
items.body: Analytics compare scheduled and actual durations by visit type and provider, so leadership can see when new OB intakes or annual exams run long and adjust the template before the delay spreads to the rest of the day.

faqs.q: How should an OB/GYN practice schedule prenatal visits?
faqs.a: Most practices follow a cadence based on gestational age: roughly every four weeks until about 28 weeks, every two weeks until about 36 weeks, then weekly until delivery. High-risk patients often need more. clinIQ books the series from the due date and keeps testing such as the anatomy ultrasound and glucose screening inside its window, so nothing depends on staff counting weeks. Read more in our guide to [prenatal visit scheduling](/blog/prenatal-visit-scheduling-optimization).

faqs.q: Can obstetric and gynecology visits share one schedule?
faqs.a: Yes. clinIQ uses separate templates for each visit type on the same provider schedule. Prenatal returns, annual exams and office procedures each carry their own length, room and staff requirements. Practices can also set aside sessions for procedures only, so a colposcopy clinic is not broken up by routine visits.

faqs.q: What happens to the schedule when the OB is called to a delivery?
faqs.a: Staff see every remaining appointment for that physician in the provider view. They can move short visits to a midwife or partner physician who has open time and contact patients who need the same physician. Patients are told before they arrive, which keeps the waiting room from filling with people who will not be seen.

faqs.q: Does clinIQ replace our EHR scheduling?
faqs.a: It can work alongside it or replace it, depending on your EHR and preferences. Many OB/GYN practices use clinIQ for templates, prenatal series, waitlists and scheduling rules while appointments sync to the EHR for clinical documentation. Integration keeps both systems consistent, so staff do not enter the same appointment twice.

check-in/preventive-cardiology.metaDescription: Preventive cardiology check-in that collects family history, medications, home blood pressure readings and lab status before the visit. See how it works.
check-in/preventive-cardiology.h1: Digital Check-In for Preventive Cardiology Clinics
check-in/preventive-cardiology.subtitle: clinIQ check-in gathers the history, medication list and risk factor details a prevention visit depends on before the patient arrives, so the visit starts with the data in hand.
check-in/preventive-cardiology.problemHeading: Why Prevention Visits Start Without the Data
check-in/preventive-cardiology.problemStatement: Preventive cardiology runs on information the patient brings. Family history of early heart disease, smoking status, current statins and other lipid drugs, supplements, home blood pressure readings and whether recent labs were drawn all shape risk assessment and treatment. On paper, that history is incomplete or illegible, the medication list is out of date and home readings stay on the patient's phone. Staff spend rooming time collecting it, and physicians make decisions with gaps they only find mid-visit.
check-in/preventive-cardiology.solutionHeading: Risk Factor Intake Before the Patient Arrives
check-in/preventive-cardiology.solutionStatement: clinIQ sends check-in by app, text or email ahead of the visit. Patients confirm demographics and insurance, photograph a new insurance card, update their medication list and complete the practice's prevention questionnaires, including family history, lifestyle and recent home blood pressure readings. They confirm whether ordered labs were drawn. Responses flow to the chart. When something is missing, such as labs not done, staff see an alert in time to act.

workflow.h2: How a Prevention Visit Check-In Works in clinIQ
workflow.intro: Most of the intake work happens at home, and the front desk only handles the exceptions.

steps.title: Check-in sent ahead
steps.body: A day before the appointment, the patient gets a push notification or a text or email link. They confirm the visit or reschedule from their phone. Patients who need fasting labs or other prep can get those instructions in the same message, as set by the practice.

steps.title: History and risk factors collected
steps.body: The patient completes the practice's questionnaires: family history of premature heart disease, smoking and activity, diet and current symptoms. Returning patients see prior answers pre-filled and only update what changed. That keeps completion high on repeat visits, which prevention patients have many of.

steps.title: Medications and readings captured
steps.body: Patients review their medication list, including statins, other lipid therapies, blood pressure drugs and supplements. They enter recent home blood pressure readings in the practice's form. Staff start the visit with an up-to-date list rather than reading pill bottles in the exam room.

steps.title: Exceptions flagged
steps.body: When the patient arrives, the [patient flow dashboard](/features/patient-flow) shows them as checked in. If labs were not drawn, insurance could not be verified or a consent is unsigned, staff see a specific alert and resolve it before rooming, not after the physician walks in.

items.title: Configurable risk questionnaires
items.body: Practices build their own family history, lifestyle and symptom forms. Answers land in the provider's view of the chart before the encounter, so risk discussions start from complete information instead of a rushed verbal history.

items.title: Medication reconciliation at home
items.body: Patients confirm or edit their medication list at home, including supplements and lipid therapies. Rooming staff verify the list rather than rebuild it, and changes since the last visit are easy to spot.

items.title: Lab status confirmation
items.body: A check-in question asks whether ordered labs were completed. A no triggers an alert, so staff can arrange a draw or adjust the visit before the physician is waiting on results that do not exist.

items.title: Three ways to check in
items.body: Patients use the clinIQ app, a web link or the waiting room kiosk. All three channels update the same record, and staff can step in to help older patients at the kiosk when needed.

items.title: Copay and insurance capture
items.body: Insurance card photos and copay payment happen during check-in. This reduces front desk work and keeps private details, such as date of birth and balances, from being discussed out loud at the counter.

faqs.q: What should patients complete before a preventive cardiology visit?
faqs.a: Usually demographics and insurance, a current medication list including supplements, family history of heart disease, smoking and lifestyle questions, symptom screening and any home blood pressure readings. Confirming whether ordered labs were drawn also helps. clinIQ lets the practice build these forms and send them ahead of the visit so the data is in the chart before rooming.

faqs.q: Can patients enter home blood pressure readings during check-in?
faqs.a: Yes. Practices can add a form where patients enter recent home readings before the visit. The responses appear for the provider alongside the rest of the intake, so the physician sees out-of-office numbers next to the reading taken in clinic. For ongoing monitoring between visits, practices can also look at [remote therapeutic monitoring](/features/rtm).

faqs.q: What if a patient arrives without completing check-in?
faqs.a: They can check in at the waiting room kiosk by name and date of birth or by scanning a driver's license. The kiosk runs the same forms as the app. Staff see on the dashboard who has arrived, who is still in progress and who needs help, so no one is missed.

faqs.q: How do digital check-in completion rates hold up with older patients?
faqs.a: Many older patients use smartphones every day and complete check-in without help. Pre-filled answers for returning patients and short forms keep completion high. Staff remain available at the kiosk for those who need assistance, and they see on the dashboard who is stuck. Our article on [check-in completion rates](/blog/check-in-completion-rates) covers what moves the number.

patient-flow/wound-care.metaTitle: Wound Care Center Patient Flow Software
patient-flow/wound-care.metaDescription: Track debridement rooms, hyperbaric chambers and dressing changes on one live board, so a wound care center stays on schedule. Book a demo for your center.
patient-flow/wound-care.h1: Patient Flow Software for Wound Care Centers
patient-flow/wound-care.subtitle: See every exam room, every hyperbaric chamber and every patient waiting on a dressing change in one live view, so a long debridement doesn't quietly push back the afternoon dive schedule.
patient-flow/wound-care.problemHeading: Why Wound Care Flow Breaks Down
patient-flow/wound-care.problemStatement: A wound care center runs several schedules at once. Weekly debridement visits range from a quick compression re-wrap to a long sharp debridement with photos and measurements. Hyperbaric sessions run a fixed length and can't be shortened, so a late or unprepared patient delays the chamber. New consults may need a same-day ABI. Nurses move between rooms with supply carts while providers wait for wounds to be undressed and measured. Without a shared view, the coordinator learns about a backup only when patients start asking.
patient-flow/wound-care.solutionHeading: One Board for Rooms, Chambers and Patients
patient-flow/wound-care.solutionStatement: clinIQ shows every patient's status from arrival through checkout, and every room's state: available, occupied, in turnover or blocked. Chambers appear alongside exam rooms, so the coordinator sees the HBO, debridement and consult tracks on one screen. Nurses tap a status when a wound is undressed and ready, and the provider's queue shows the next patient and room. Wait times are color-coded, and stale statuses raise an alert, so a forgotten update or an overrun is visible within minutes.

workflow.h2: How a Wound Care Visit Moves Through clinIQ
workflow.intro: A typical weekly visit for a diabetic foot ulcer patient who is also in a course of hyperbaric oxygen.

steps.title: Arrival and pre-treatment prep
steps.body: The patient checks in and appears in the waiting queue with visit type and track. For an HBO patient, staff can see the chamber time they need to make, so the nurse starts pre-treatment checks, such as vitals and a blood glucose check for diabetic patients, early enough to protect it.

steps.title: Rooming and wound prep
steps.body: The nurse rooms the patient, removes the dressing and any offloading device, and takes photos and measurements. One tap marks the patient ready, and the room shows as occupied with the assigned provider. Nobody has to walk the hall to say the wound is ready to look at.

steps.title: Provider debridement
steps.body: The provider sees the patient at the top of their queue with the room number. Room wait is tracked from the moment the patient was marked ready, so a provider held up by a long sharp debridement is visible to the coordinator, who can move a simpler follow-up to another provider.

steps.title: Dressing, chamber and turnover
steps.body: After debridement, the nurse applies the dressing or compression wrap, and the patient moves to the chamber queue or to checkout. The exam room flips to turnover for cleaning and restocking, and the turnover timer shows when a room has sat unready too long.

capabilities.h2: Built for Wound Care Patient Flow

items.title: Chambers tracked like rooms
items.body: Hyperbaric chambers carry the same available, occupied, turnover and blocked states as exam rooms. Coordinators see chamber status next to the clinic and can tell right away whether a late arrival will affect the next session.

items.title: Visit types on the board
items.body: Debridements, total contact cast changes, skin substitute applications and new consults are labeled on the board, so a long procedure isn't mistaken for a quick re-wrap. Patients whose status hasn't changed in too long raise an alert.

items.title: Nurse-to-provider handoff
items.body: A single tap tells the provider the wound is exposed, measured and ready. Providers stop knocking on doors to check, and patients spend less time sitting with an open wound waiting for someone to come in.

items.title: Turnover visibility
items.body: Wound care rooms need more cleaning and restocking than a standard exam room. Turnover timers show where rooms are stuck, a common source of lost capacity. Our guide to [room status visibility](/blog/room-status-visibility) explains why it matters.

items.title: Wait time by segment
items.body: Waits are split into lobby time and time in the room before the provider arrives, by provider and visit type. That shows whether delays come from rooming, provider time or turnover, so template changes rest on what happened.

faqs.q: How do wound care centers schedule hyperbaric chamber time and clinic visits together?
faqs.a: Most run separate tracks: one grid for chambers, one for debridement rooms and one for consults, with a coordinator watching all three. clinIQ's patient flow board shows every chamber and exam room in real time, so when a debridement runs long or an HBO patient arrives late, the coordinator sees the conflict and adjusts before it spreads through the day.

faqs.q: How long does a wound care visit take?
faqs.a: It depends on the visit type. A compression re-wrap for a venous ulcer can be brief, while a sharp debridement with photos, measurements and a new dressing takes much longer, and a new consult with vascular testing longer still. Tracking actual times by visit type, rather than using one default slot length, is how centers build a schedule that holds.

faqs.q: What causes delays in a wound care center?
faqs.a: The usual causes are waiting for wounds to be undressed and measured before the provider can see them, a provider held up by a complex debridement, rooms left in turnover after messy dressing changes, and chamber sessions that can't start on time. Real-time status makes each one visible as it happens. Our [wound care center patient flow guide](/blog/wound-care-center-patient-flow) covers each in detail.

faqs.q: Do we need wall displays to use patient flow in a wound clinic?
faqs.a: No. The board runs on existing desktops, tablets and phones. Many centers add a wall display at the nurse station or near the chambers, because nurses moving between rooms in gloves can glance at it without logging in to a computer. Status updates take a single tap on any device.

scheduling/neurology.metaTitle: Neurology Scheduling Software for EEG and EMG
scheduling/neurology.metaDescription: Neurology scheduling that sizes new patient visits correctly, books EEG and EMG on the right equipment and keeps Botox and infusion intervals on time.
scheduling/neurology.h1: Neurology Scheduling Software for Long Visits and Testing
scheduling/neurology.subtitle: clinIQ gives neurology practices templates for long new patient visits, equipment-aware booking for EEG and EMG, and recurring series for treatments that run on fixed intervals.
scheduling/neurology.problemHeading: Why Neurology Access Is So Hard to Manage
scheduling/neurology.problemStatement: Neurology has long new patient waits in many markets, and the schedule is part of the cause. A new headache, seizure or neuropathy evaluation takes far longer than a follow-up, yet many templates give them the same slot. EEG and EMG with nerve conduction studies need specific rooms, machines and technologists. Botox for chronic migraine runs on a 12-week cycle, and MS infusions follow their own interval. Urgent referrals, such as a new seizure, compete for the same scarce openings.
scheduling/neurology.solutionHeading: A Schedule That Matches Neurology Work
scheduling/neurology.solutionStatement: clinIQ sizes each neurology visit type to its real length and attaches the rooms, equipment and staff it needs. An EMG template reserves the EMG machine and the provider. An EEG template reserves the EEG room and a technologist, with prep time for electrode placement. Recurring treatments book as a series on their interval. Rules hold a small amount of capacity for urgent new referrals, and the waitlist fills cancellations from the long new patient queue.

workflow.h2: How a Neurology Referral Moves Through clinIQ
workflow.intro: A referral becomes a correctly sized visit, the right test slot and, where needed, a treatment series.

steps.title: Referral triaged
steps.body: The scheduler picks the template that matches the referral reason. A new seizure or rapidly progressing symptom goes into held urgent capacity. A routine new headache evaluation goes into a long new patient slot. Neither one is squeezed into a short follow-up block that would put the clinic behind.

steps.title: Testing booked to equipment
steps.body: If the provider orders an EEG or EMG with nerve conduction studies, the scheduler books it on the template that reserves the right room, machine and staff. clinIQ blocks only the times when those resources are free, so two studies never collide on one machine.

steps.title: Treatment series set
steps.body: Patients on Botox for chronic migraine are booked as a recurring series on the 12-week cycle, so they are not under-treated or seen too early for coverage. Infusion patients get a series that matches their drug's schedule. Staff manage the whole series as a group.

steps.title: Openings filled from the queue
steps.body: When a new patient cancels, the [waitlist](/features/scheduling) offers the opening by text to the next matching patient, ranked by how long they have waited. A yes reply books it. Long new patient slots rarely go empty, which matters most where the wait is longest.

items.title: Long visit templates
items.body: New patient, follow-up, procedure and testing visits each carry their own length. Analytics show where new evaluations run past their template, by provider and by referral type, so leadership can resize them with data.

items.title: Equipment and technologist rules
items.body: EEG, EMG and other testing templates reserve the machine, the room and the technologist together. Prep and cleanup time, such as electrode placement and removal, is built in, so the next study starts on time.

items.title: Interval-based series
items.body: Botox for migraine, infusions and routine MS or epilepsy follow-ups book as recurring series. Staff can see when a patient falls off their interval before it becomes a gap in care.

items.title: Overbooking limits by visit type
items.body: Rules allow short follow-ups to double up in time slots where no-shows are likely, and block overbooking of long new patient visits entirely. The worst-case delay for the neurologist stays small even when everyone arrives.

items.title: Provider preparation view
items.body: Neurologists see tomorrow's schedule with visit types and flags, such as an interpreter need or a pending study result. They can request blocked time for procedures, and the request routes to scheduling staff.

faqs.q: How long should a new neurology patient appointment be?
faqs.a: New neurology evaluations usually need much more time than follow-ups because they involve a detailed history and a full neurological exam. The right length depends on your providers and referral mix. clinIQ lets you set a template per visit type and then compares scheduled and actual times, so you can resize templates based on your own data rather than guesses.

faqs.q: How do neurology practices reduce new patient wait times?
faqs.a: Most of the gain comes from using capacity that already exists. Correctly sized templates stop the day from running over. Waitlist automation fills cancellations within hours instead of losing them. Overbooking rules for short follow-ups recover no-show slots. Held urgent capacity keeps critical referrals from waiting behind routine ones. clinIQ handles each of these on the schedule your staff already use.

faqs.q: Can clinIQ schedule Botox for chronic migraine every 12 weeks?
faqs.a: Yes. Staff book the injections as a recurring series on a 12-week interval with a consistent day and time. The full series is visible and can be moved as a group. Payer authorization for each cycle is tracked separately in the [pre-authorization module](/features/pre-auth), so the visit and the approval stay in step.

faqs.q: Can EEG and EMG be booked without double-booking equipment?
faqs.a: Yes. Each testing template specifies the room, equipment and staff it requires. clinIQ shows only times when all of them are free. If a practice has one EMG machine shared by two neurologists, the schedule reflects that limit automatically, and an EEG cannot be booked when no technologist is on shift.

lobbyview/primary-care.metaTitle: Waiting Room Display for Primary Care Practices
lobbyview/primary-care.metaDescription: Show primary care patients their place in line on a lobby screen without names, even with same-day sick visits and several providers. See it in a demo.
lobbyview/primary-care.h1: A Waiting Room Display Built for Busy Primary Care Lobbies
lobbyview/primary-care.subtitle: LobbyView shows patients where they stand on a lobby screen without names, so a physical patient isn't left wondering why someone who arrived later went back first.
lobbyview/primary-care.problemHeading: Why Primary Care Lobbies Feel Unfair
lobbyview/primary-care.problemStatement: A primary care lobby holds patients for several providers at once, plus same-day sick visits added to the schedule, lab-only draws and patients in for a quick vaccine. From a waiting chair, the order looks random. Someone who arrived at 9:40 for a physical watches three people go back ahead of them and decides they've been forgotten. They ask at the desk, which interrupts check-in for the next patient. In flu season the lobby fills faster, the questions multiply, and some patients leave and call back to reschedule.
lobbyview/primary-care.solutionHeading: Wait Status Patients Can See Without Asking
lobbyview/primary-care.solutionStatement: LobbyView puts the queue on a lobby screen without using names. It draws on clinIQ [patient flow](/features/patient-flow) and check-in, so it reflects what is actually happening: who has arrived, who has been roomed and where each waiting patient stands. Patients can see that the line is moving and that they are in it. The front desk stops answering the same question all morning, and the staff rooming patients work from the same live data that drives the screen.

workflow.h2: How LobbyView Works in a Primary Care Office
workflow.intro: The screen updates from the same check-in and rooming events your staff already record.

steps.title: Patient checks in
steps.body: The patient checks in on their phone before arriving or at a kiosk in the lobby. As soon as check-in is complete, they join the queue and appear on the lobby screen without their name, so nobody else in the room learns who is there or why.

steps.title: The screen shows position
steps.body: Patients see where they stand. Because the order follows live patient flow, a same-day sick visit or a lab draw going back first no longer looks like someone cutting the line. Patients can judge whether there is time to step out for a call.

steps.title: The MA rooms the patient
steps.body: When a medical assistant rooms the patient for vitals, the status changes on the flow board and the lobby display at the same moment. Nothing extra is entered for the screen, so it stays current through the 8 AM rush and the late-afternoon catch-up.

steps.title: The manager reviews the day
steps.body: Lobby wait time is recorded for every visit. With [practice analytics](/features/analytics), the manager can see which providers, visit types and hours produce the longest waits and adjust the template, for example by holding more same-day slots on Monday mornings. Those changes show up on the lobby screen the next week.

capabilities.h2: Built for Primary Care Waiting Rooms

items.title: No names on screen
items.body: The display shows wait status without using names. That protects privacy in a lobby where neighbors, coworkers and relatives often see the same practice. Nothing on the screen reveals the reason for anyone's visit, so a lab draw and a mental health follow-up look the same.

items.title: Live from patient flow
items.body: LobbyView reads from check-in and rooming status, not a separate list. When the front desk or an MA updates the board, the screen reflects it with no double entry. It stays accurate through a full day of add-ons and walk-ins.

items.title: Fewer interruptions at the desk
items.body: When patients can see where they stand, the "how much longer" questions drop. Front desk staff can stay focused on insurance problems, phone lines and same-day scheduling requests. Patients who do come to the desk usually have a real need.

items.title: One queue for mixed visit types
items.body: Physicals, chronic care follow-ups, same-day sick visits and nurse visits move through one live queue, so the order on screen matches what patients see happening around them. No one reads a nurse visit going first as being skipped.

faqs.q: Should a primary care office display wait times in the waiting room?
faqs.a: For most practices, yes. Patients tolerate a wait far better when they can see where they stand than when they hear nothing. A display that shows queue position without names reduces walkouts and front desk interruptions. It must update from live data, because an out-of-date screen does more harm than no screen. Our post on [waiting room complaints](/blog/waiting-room-complaints) explains why.

faqs.q: Does LobbyView show patient names?
faqs.a: No. LobbyView displays wait status on the lobby screen without using names, and it doesn't show the reason for the visit. Patients can see where they stand without anyone else in the room learning who they are, which matters in a community practice where people often know each other. Staff can still call patients back the way they do today.

faqs.q: How does a waiting room display handle multiple providers?
faqs.a: Patients in a primary care lobby are waiting for different providers, so a single first-come list would be misleading. LobbyView draws on clinIQ patient flow, which tracks each provider's queue, so the display reflects the order patients are actually being roomed. A patient whose provider is running behind sees that, instead of watching others go back and assuming they were skipped.

faqs.q: How do I stop patients asking how much longer at the front desk?
faqs.a: Answer the question before it is asked. Patients ask because they can't see progress. A lobby screen showing their place in line, updated as patients are roomed, removes most of those trips to the desk. The questions that remain are usually about a real delay, such as a provider running behind, which staff can address directly.

pre-auth/wound-care.metaDescription: Track HBO, skin substitute and NPWT authorizations, count down approved treatments and get alerts before coverage lapses. See clinIQ for your wound center.
pre-auth/wound-care.h1: Prior Authorization Software for Wound Care Centers
pre-auth/wound-care.subtitle: clinIQ tracks every authorization for hyperbaric oxygen, skin substitutes and negative pressure wound therapy, counts down approved treatments and alerts staff before a course runs out of coverage.
pre-auth/wound-care.problemHeading: Why Wound Care Authorizations Go Wrong
pre-auth/wound-care.problemStatement: Wound care's most effective therapies are the ones payers scrutinize most. Hyperbaric oxygen for a diabetic foot ulcer requires documented wound severity and a failed course of standard care. Skin substitutes require serial measurements showing the wound hasn't responded. NPWT has its own documentation rules. Then the approval covers a set number of treatments or applications, which get used up in a busy weekly schedule. When no one counts them, a patient arrives for a session that is no longer covered, and the claim is denied after the fact.
pre-auth/wound-care.solutionHeading: Every Wound Care Auth, Tracked to the Last Treatment
pre-auth/wound-care.solutionStatement: clinIQ keeps each authorization on one dashboard with its status, authorization number, valid dates and approved units. Templates for HBO, skin substitutes and NPWT pull in diagnosis codes, wound measurements and prior treatment history, and pre-submission checks flag gaps such as missing conservative care documentation before the request goes out. As treatments are scheduled and completed, clinIQ counts them down and alerts staff before the count or the date runs out, with the renewal queued from the original request.

workflow.h2: How a Wound Care Authorization Moves Through clinIQ
workflow.intro: An example: a Wagner grade 3 diabetic foot ulcer referred for hyperbaric oxygen therapy.

steps.title: Build the request
steps.body: Staff select the patient and the HBO template. clinIQ fills in demographics, diagnosis codes, wound grade, measurements over time and the standard care already delivered, such as offloading, debridement and infection management. A physician reviews and signs the letter of medical necessity before it is submitted.

steps.title: Check before submitting
steps.body: Pre-submission verification looks for the gaps behind most wound care denials: no documented duration of standard care, no vascular assessment on file, or measurements that don't show the non-healing period. Staff fix the gap before the payer sees it, not after a denial letter arrives.

steps.title: Track the approval
steps.body: Once approved, the authorization number, valid dates and number of approved treatments are recorded. Each completed session counts down against the total, so staff can see how many remain before the patient's next week of treatments is confirmed on the schedule.

steps.title: Renew or stop on time
steps.body: When remaining treatments or the end date reach the thresholds you set, the responsible staff member gets an alert. If the wound needs more sessions, the renewal is queued with the original documentation and the latest measurements, ready for review well before coverage ends.

capabilities.h2: Built for Wound Care Prior Authorization

items.title: Therapy-specific templates
items.body: Separate letter templates for hyperbaric oxygen, skin substitutes and negative pressure wound therapy reflect what each payer review looks for, and they populate from wound data already documented. Staff edit a populated draft instead of writing from a blank page.

items.title: Treatment and application countdown
items.body: Each authorization records its approved sessions, applications or units. clinIQ counts them down as visits happen, so a patient doesn't receive a treatment the payer never approved. Coordinators see remaining sessions next to the schedule.

items.title: Expiration alerts
items.body: Alerts reach the right person on a schedule you set before an authorization lapses. Our guide to [tracking prior authorization expirations](/blog/track-prior-authorization-expirations) shows how practices choose their thresholds. Medication and therapy auths can carry earlier alerts.

items.title: Denial and appeal tracking
items.body: Denial reasons are recorded, appeal templates match the reason, and appeal deadlines are tracked. Peer-to-peer reviews are scheduled when a written appeal isn't enough to overturn the decision. Outcomes feed back into which requests need more work before submission.

items.title: One view across payers
items.body: A single dashboard shows every active wound care authorization by payer, provider and therapy, sorted by expiration date and remaining units. It replaces the spreadsheet that only one coordinator understands.

faqs.q: Does hyperbaric oxygen therapy for a diabetic foot ulcer need prior authorization?
faqs.a: Many commercial and Medicare Advantage plans require it, and Medicare has specific coverage criteria. Under Medicare's national coverage determination for HBO (NCD 20.29), the diabetic lower-extremity wound generally must be Wagner grade 3 or higher and must have failed an adequate course of standard wound therapy, meaning no measurable healing over at least 30 days. Documenting both clearly is the core of an approvable request.

faqs.q: What documentation do payers want for skin substitutes?
faqs.a: Payers generally want evidence that the wound has not responded to standard care, shown through serial measurements of length, width and depth over several weeks. They also look for documented offloading or compression, infection control and adequate blood flow. Each application usually counts against a limit, so tracking applications used matters as much as the initial approval.

faqs.q: How do I keep track of how many HBO treatments are left on an authorization?
faqs.a: Record the number of approved treatments with the authorization and count down each completed session. clinIQ does this automatically as visits are completed and alerts staff when only a few treatments remain or the end date is near. That way a renewal goes in before the patient arrives for a session that wouldn't be covered.

faqs.q: What are common reasons wound care prior authorizations are denied?
faqs.a: The most common are missing documentation of the standard care already tried and how long it lasted, wound grade or measurements that don't meet the payer's criteria, no vascular assessment, and requests that exceed frequency or application limits. Our [wound care prior auth guide](/blog/wound-care-prior-auth-hbo-dressings) walks through the criteria for each therapy.

scheduling/gastroenterology.h1: Gastroenterology Scheduling for Clinic and Endoscopy Days
scheduling/gastroenterology.subtitle: clinIQ books office visits and endoscopy cases on templates that know procedure rooms, sedation, prep timing and recovery, so a GI day runs to plan.
scheduling/gastroenterology.problemHeading: Where GI Procedure Days Lose Time
scheduling/gastroenterology.problemStatement: A gastroenterology schedule splits between clinic visits and endoscopy, and the endoscopy side is fragile. Colonoscopy, EGD and combined cases need different lengths, a room, nursing and often anesthesia. Patients must follow bowel prep, adjust certain medications and bring an escort if sedated. When prep fails or a driver falls through, the case cancels late and the room sits empty. Surveillance colonoscopies are due years after the last one, and those recalls are easy to lose.
scheduling/gastroenterology.solutionStatement: clinIQ gives each GI case its own template with length, room, staff and turnover time. Combined EGD and colonoscopy cases get a longer block than either alone. Reminders go out ahead of the procedure, and staff confirm the escort before the day. When a case cancels late, the waitlist offers the slot to patients who are already cleared and willing to come on short notice. Surveillance patients are booked from recall so they come back when due.

workflow.h2: How a Colonoscopy Moves Through clinIQ Scheduling
workflow.intro: From the referral to the recall, each step is booked with the rooms and time the case actually needs.

steps.title: Referral routed
steps.body: Staff decide whether the patient needs an office consult first or qualifies for direct-access screening under your criteria. clinIQ books the matching template: a consult visit on the clinic schedule or a screening colonoscopy on the endoscopy schedule, with sedation type noted.

steps.title: Case booked to the room
steps.body: The colonoscopy template reserves the procedure room, the endoscopist, nursing and anesthesia time where used, plus turnover. clinIQ prevents the room from being double-booked and places longer cases, such as combined EGD and colonoscopy, where the day can absorb them.

steps.title: Prep and escort confirmed
steps.body: Reminders reach the patient ahead of the procedure date with enough time to start prep, review medication instructions and arrange a ride. Patients confirm or reschedule from their phone. Staff see unconfirmed cases days ahead instead of discovering a missing driver at check-in.

steps.title: Late openings refilled
steps.body: If a case cancels, the [waitlist](/features/scheduling) texts matching patients who can be ready on short notice. A yes reply books the slot. Staff then confirm prep instructions with the new patient, so the room is used instead of sitting idle.

steps.title: Recall set
steps.body: After the procedure, the patient's next surveillance or follow-up date is set from the physician's recommendation. When the date approaches, the patient is invited to schedule, and staff can work a list of those who do not respond, so surveillance patients do not quietly drop out of care.

items.title: Case-specific templates
items.body: Screening colonoscopy, diagnostic colonoscopy, EGD, combined cases and office visits each have their own length, room, sedation and staff rules. Turnover time is part of the template, so the schedule reflects the real pace of the endoscopy suite.

items.title: Separate clinic and endoscopy schedules
items.body: A physician's office sessions and endoscopy blocks sit on one view. Schedulers can book a consult and the procedure that follows without switching systems, and the physician sees both parts of the week together.

items.title: Short-notice waitlist
items.body: Patients who can come in quickly are flagged on the waitlist. Late cancellations go to them first, which matters when a slot needs a patient who has time to prep.

items.title: Utilization analytics
items.body: Leadership sees room use, late cancellations and no-shows by procedure type, day and endoscopist, then adjusts blocks and overbooking rules. Our guide to [colonoscopy and EGD scheduling](/blog/gi-procedure-scheduling-colonoscopy-egd) covers the patterns.

faqs.q: How do GI practices reduce last-minute colonoscopy cancellations?
faqs.a: Most late cancellations come from prep problems, missing escorts or patients who forgot. Timed reminders with clear prep instructions, a confirmation step a few days ahead and an easy reschedule option address all three. clinIQ adds a short-notice waitlist so the cancellations that still happen get refilled instead of leaving the room idle.

faqs.q: How long should a colonoscopy slot be?
faqs.a: It depends on the endoscopist, sedation type, room setup and case mix. Combined EGD and colonoscopy cases need more time than either alone, and turnover must be included. clinIQ lets you set a template for each case type and compares scheduled to actual times, so the template can be adjusted from real data.

faqs.q: Can clinIQ handle direct-access screening colonoscopy?
faqs.a: Yes. Practices that book screening colonoscopy without a prior office visit can create a template for it and route eligible referrals straight to the endoscopy schedule. Patients who do not meet your direct-access criteria are booked for a consult first. The criteria are your practice's; clinIQ applies the template you choose.

faqs.q: Does clinIQ track surveillance colonoscopy recalls?
faqs.a: Yes. Staff set the follow-up date the physician recommends after each procedure. As it approaches, the patient is invited to schedule, and patients who do not respond can be worked from a list by phone. This keeps surveillance patients from being lost between visits that may be years apart. Recall lists also show leadership how many patients are overdue.

check-in/behavioral-health.h1: Private, Pre-Session Check-In for Behavioral Health Practices
check-in/behavioral-health.subtitle: Patients confirm their session, complete screeners and update insurance on their own phone before they arrive or log on. Nobody says their name across a waiting room, and the clinician starts the session with scores already in hand.
check-in/behavioral-health.problemHeading: Why Check-In Is Hard in Behavioral Health
check-in/behavioral-health.problemStatement: Behavioral health sessions run on the hour, often back to back, so a ten-minute delay at the desk comes out of a 45- or 60-minute session that can't run into the next patient's time. Patients are handed PHQ-9 or GAD-7 screeners on a clipboard in a shared lobby, which feels exposed. Many sessions are telehealth, so the front desk has no reliable signal that a patient is ready. And a sign-in sheet with names on it is the last thing a person seeking care for depression, trauma or substance use wants to see.
check-in/behavioral-health.solutionHeading: Check-In That Happens Before the Session Starts
check-in/behavioral-health.solutionStatement: clinIQ sends a check-in link or app reminder 24 hours before each appointment. Patients confirm attendance, verify demographics and insurance, sign consents and complete the screeners your practice assigns to that visit type. Responses flow into the chart, so the clinician sees this week's PHQ-9 next to last month's before the patient sits down. In-office arrivals check in on their phone or a kiosk without speaking to anyone. Telehealth patients show as ready on the [patient flow board](/features/patient-flow), so clinicians aren't left waiting in an empty video room.

workflow.h2: How a Therapy Session Check-In Moves Through clinIQ
workflow.intro: The same steps work for in-office and video sessions. Only the arrival step changes.

steps.title: Reminder and confirmation
steps.body: The day before, the patient gets a push notification, text or email with their session time and clinician. They confirm or reschedule in a tap. A reschedule frees the hour early enough for the practice to offer it to someone on the waitlist, instead of absorbing a no-show.

steps.title: Screeners and paperwork
steps.body: The patient completes the measures assigned to their visit type, such as the PHQ-9 or GAD-7, along with any consent, release of information or telehealth agreement that is due. Returning patients see their details pre-filled and confirm only what changed. Insurance card photos upload from the phone.

steps.title: Arrival without a sign-in sheet
steps.body: In the office, the patient checks in on their phone or the kiosk by the door and takes a seat. No name is written on a sheet or called across the room. The front desk sees a green status on its dashboard and steps in only when something is flagged.

steps.title: Clinician sees readiness and scores
steps.body: The clinician's queue shows the patient as arrived or, for video sessions, checked in and waiting. Screener responses are already in the chart, so a rising score or a positive answer on PHQ-9 item 9 is seen before the session begins, not discovered forty minutes in.

items.title: Measurement-based care at check-in
items.body: Assign the PHQ-9, GAD-7 or other standardized screeners by visit type and interval. Patients complete them before the session, and scores land in the chart, so trends are visible across visits without hand scoring.

items.title: No names in the lobby
items.body: Self-service check-in on phone, kiosk or web removes the clipboard and the sign-in sheet. Pair it with [LobbyView](/features/lobbyview), which shows wait status on a lobby screen without using names. Patients sit down and wait without being announced.

items.title: Telehealth arrival status
items.body: Patients check in for video sessions the same way they do for office visits. The clinician sees who is ready, and the front desk can reach out to anyone who hasn't checked in as the hour approaches.

items.title: Consents and releases on schedule
items.body: Annual consents, telehealth agreements and releases of information appear in check-in when they are due. Patients sign electronically, the documents attach to the record, and staff stop chasing signatures at the desk.

items.title: Coverage and copay before the session
items.body: Eligibility checks and copay collection happen during check-in, so money and coverage questions don't spill into therapy time. Problems show up as specific alerts for front desk or billing staff.

faqs.q: Can patients complete the PHQ-9 before a therapy appointment?
faqs.a: Yes. clinIQ can include the PHQ-9, GAD-7 or other screeners your practice uses in pre-visit check-in, sent the day before the appointment. Patients answer on their phone or computer, and responses pass into the clinical record. The clinician reviews them before the session instead of spending the first minutes on forms. You choose which visit types get each measure and how often.

faqs.q: How do I protect patient privacy at check-in in a mental health practice?
faqs.a: Remove anything in the lobby that exposes names or reasons for visit. That means no sign-in sheet, no reading dates of birth aloud and no forms filled out on a clipboard in view of others. Digital check-in lets patients confirm identity, insurance and paperwork on their own device, and a name-free lobby display answers the "how much longer" question.

faqs.q: Does digital check-in work for telehealth therapy sessions?
faqs.a: Yes. Telehealth patients get the same reminder and check-in flow as in-office patients, including screeners and consents. When they finish, their status updates on the clinician's dashboard, so the clinician knows the patient is ready before opening the video visit. Staff can also see who hasn't checked in as the session time approaches and contact them.

faqs.q: Can digital check-in help reduce no-shows in behavioral health?
faqs.a: It helps by making cancelling easy and early. Each check-in reminder asks the patient to confirm or reschedule, and a reschedule frees the slot while there is still time to offer it to a waitlisted patient. It does not replace outreach to patients who disengage, but it gives staff an early, clear signal. Our guide to [behavioral health no-shows](/blog/behavioral-health-no-shows) covers the rest.

analytics/medical-oncology.h1: Oncology Analytics for Chair Utilization and Infusion Turnaround
analytics/medical-oncology.subtitle: clinIQ measures every step between lab draw and chair so medical oncology practices can see where treatment days lose time and fill chairs they already have.
analytics/medical-oncology.problemStatement: A medical oncology treatment day runs through lab draw, results, provider visit, treatment approval, pharmacy mixing and finally the chair. Each handoff adds minutes, and nobody owns the total. Chairs sit empty in the morning while patients wait on pharmacy, then the afternoon runs late. Regimen lengths vary from a short injection to a full-day infusion, so a chair calendar that looks full can still have hours of idle time. Without timestamps at each step, managers argue about causes instead of fixing them.
analytics/medical-oncology.solutionHeading: Timestamps at Every Handoff, Reported by Chair
analytics/medical-oncology.solutionStatement: clinIQ records when each patient checks in, finishes labs, sees the provider, gets cleared for treatment and sits down in a chair. Analytics turns those timestamps into lab-to-chair time, provider-to-chair time and chair idle time, broken out by day, regimen length and provider. The live dashboard shows which chairs are open now and which patients are waiting on pharmacy. Historical reports show whether the 10 a.m. bottleneck is a staffing problem or a scheduling template problem, so changes target the real cause.

workflow.h2: How an Infusion Day Is Measured in clinIQ
workflow.intro: Each status change becomes a data point. Here is how a typical treatment visit turns into reports.

steps.title: Check-in and lab draw
steps.body: The patient checks in and moves to the lab queue. clinIQ starts the visit clock and logs when the draw finishes. The waiting-for-labs segment shows up in reports by hour, so managers can see whether early arrivals pile up before the lab is fully staffed.

steps.title: Provider visit and treatment clearance
steps.body: When the oncologist or APP sees the patient and clears treatment, staff mark the status change. Analytics separates time spent waiting for results from time spent waiting for the provider. Those are different problems with different owners, and the report keeps them apart.

steps.title: Pharmacy and chair assignment
steps.body: The patient waits while the drug is prepared. clinIQ tracks the gap between clearance and chair seating, which is where many infusion days lose the most time. The live view flags patients past your threshold so the charge nurse can call pharmacy before the delay spreads.

steps.title: Treatment and chair turnover
steps.body: Chair start and end times feed chair utilization reports. clinIQ compares actual chair time with the scheduled slot for each regimen length and shows how long chairs sit empty between patients. Read more in our guide to [infusion chair utilization and scheduling](/blog/infusion-center-scheduling-chair-utilization).

capabilities.h2: Reports Built for Medical Oncology Operations

items.title: Chair utilization by hour
items.body: See what share of available chair hours had a patient in them, hour by hour and chair by chair. Morning gaps and late-afternoon overruns become visible, which helps when rebuilding templates around long and short regimens.

items.title: Lab-to-chair and clearance-to-chair time
items.body: Track the two intervals that drive most infusion delays. Trend them weekly to confirm whether a change in lab staffing, result review or pharmacy workflow actually moved the number, instead of assuming it did.

items.title: Scheduled versus actual regimen time
items.body: Compare how long treatments are booked for against how long they actually take in the chair. Regimens that consistently run over get flagged, so schedulers can adjust slot length based on evidence instead of guessing.

items.title: Scheduled and exported reports
items.body: Send a daily chair summary to the infusion nurse manager and a monthly trend report to practice leadership automatically. Export any report to Excel, CSV or PDF for service line reviews and capacity planning meetings.

faqs.q: How do you measure infusion chair utilization?
faqs.a: Divide the hours chairs were occupied by the hours chairs were available during operating time. clinIQ calculates this from actual seat and release timestamps, not from the schedule, so it reflects what happened. Reports break utilization out by hour, day of week and chair, which shows where idle time concentrates and whether it comes from late starts, early finishes or gaps between patients.

faqs.q: What causes long waits before chemotherapy starts?
faqs.a: Most waits come from a chain of dependencies: lab results, the provider visit, treatment approval and drug preparation. Any one can stall the day. clinIQ times each segment separately, so you can see whether patients mostly wait on results, on the provider or on pharmacy. That tells you which team and which process to change first.

faqs.q: Does clinIQ analytics replace our EHR's oncology reports?
faqs.a: No. Your EHR holds the clinical record, regimens and orders. clinIQ adds the operational layer the EHR does not capture well: where the patient is, how long each step took and how chairs and rooms are used. Many practices use both, with clinIQ answering the throughput and capacity questions that clinical reports leave open.

faqs.q: Can we compare infusion performance across locations?
faqs.a: Yes. Multi-site oncology groups can view chair utilization, lab-to-chair time and wait times by location, compare sites side by side and roll results up to the whole organization. This helps leadership decide where to add chairs, nursing staff or pharmacy capacity, and which site's workflow the other sites should consider copying.

lobbyview/neurology.metaDescription: Neurology visits range from short follow-ups to long new evaluations, so lobby order looks random. Show patients their place, without names. See a demo.
lobbyview/neurology.h1: Waiting Room Display Software for Neurology Practices
lobbyview/neurology.subtitle: Patients with long new evaluations, EEG appointments and Botox visits share one lobby. LobbyView shows each of them, and the caregivers with them, where they stand without displaying names.
lobbyview/neurology.problemStatement: A neurology lobby mixes very different visits. A new seizure or memory evaluation can take well over an hour, a stable MS follow-up is short, and a Botox injection for chronic migraine is a set procedure. When one new evaluation runs long, the next hour backs up. Many patients arrive with a caregiver, and many have fatigue, mobility limits or cognitive symptoms that make an unexplained wait harder. Caregivers go to the desk to ask, and staff lose time they need for scheduling EEGs and returning calls.
lobbyview/neurology.solutionHeading: A Calm, Name-Free View of the Queue
lobbyview/neurology.solutionStatement: LobbyView shows patients and caregivers their place in the queue on a lobby screen, without names. It draws on clinIQ [patient flow](/features/patient-flow), so when a new evaluation runs long, the screen reflects the real order instead of a printed schedule. A caregiver can see there is time to move the car or get a coffee. Patients with memory symptoms don't have to hold their place in their head. Front desk staff get back the time they spent answering the same question.

workflow.h2: How LobbyView Works in a Neurology Clinic
workflow.intro: The display follows the same check-in and rooming events your team already records.

steps.title: Check-in for patient and caregiver
steps.body: The patient, or a caregiver on their behalf, checks in on a phone before the visit or at the lobby kiosk. Once check-in is complete, the patient joins the queue and appears on the lobby display without their name. Forms are done before arrival, not balanced on a lap in the lobby.

steps.title: The queue reflects long visits
steps.body: If a 90-minute new evaluation is running over, patients waiting for that neurologist see their position hold instead of guessing. Patients waiting for a different provider or for an EEG tech keep moving. The order on screen matches what is actually happening in the clinic.

steps.title: Rooming updates the screen
steps.body: When a medical assistant brings a patient back for vitals, or a tech takes them for an EEG, the status changes on the flow board and the lobby display together. Staff never update the screen separately, so it stays accurate even on the busiest clinic days.

steps.title: Patterns reviewed after clinic
steps.body: Lobby wait time is recorded for every visit. With [practice analytics](/features/analytics), managers can see which visit types, providers and days create the longest waits, and use that to set realistic slot lengths for new evaluations and procedure visits. Changes are visible on the lobby screen the following week.

items.title: No names, no visit reasons
items.body: The lobby screen shows wait status without using names. Nothing on the display tells other patients who is there for epilepsy, dementia or MS care. Patients and caregivers can watch their position without announcing anything about themselves.

items.title: Easier for patients with memory symptoms
items.body: A visible place in line means a patient with memory or attention problems doesn't need to remember what the front desk said twenty minutes ago. Caregivers can check the screen instead of asking.

items.title: Reflects every queue
items.body: Neurologist visits, EEG testing and Botox procedure visits move at different speeds. Because LobbyView follows live patient flow, the screen shows how each queue is really moving. A patient waiting for a tech isn't confused by a neurologist running late.

items.title: Fewer desk interruptions
items.body: Neurology front desk staff also schedule EEGs, coordinate imaging and field medication calls. Fewer "how much longer" questions leaves them time for that work. Caregivers get answers from the screen, and the phones get answered.

items.title: Status, not entertainment
items.body: LobbyView is a status display, not a video loop. When choosing anything else that runs on lobby screens, avoid flashing or strobing content, which can trigger seizures in patients with photosensitive epilepsy.

faqs.q: Why do neurology appointments run behind?
faqs.a: Mostly because visit lengths vary so much. A new evaluation for seizures, neuropathy or memory loss takes far longer than an established follow-up, and actual times often run past the slot. One long new patient can delay the rest of the session. Separate slot types and real-time tracking help. Our [neurology patient flow guide](/blog/neurology-patient-flow) covers how to build them.

faqs.q: Is a waiting room display a good idea for a neurology practice?
faqs.a: Yes, if it protects privacy and stays current. LobbyView shows queue position without names, so no one learns who is there or why. Updates come from live patient flow rather than manual entry. Practices should keep lobby screens free of flashing or rapidly changing graphics out of consideration for patients with photosensitive epilepsy.

faqs.q: How can a neurology clinic help caregivers during long waits?
faqs.a: Give them information they can see without asking. Caregivers often manage transport, medications and the patient's comfort at the same time. A lobby display showing the patient's place in line lets them decide whether to step out, and digital check-in lets them complete forms on the patient's behalf before arrival instead of at the desk.

faqs.q: Does LobbyView work with EEG and testing schedules?
faqs.a: LobbyView shows what clinIQ patient flow is tracking. When your EEG room or testing area is set up in patient flow, patients waiting for testing appear in the queue, and their status updates when a tech brings them back. That keeps the lobby view accurate for patients who are not waiting for a neurologist.

analytics/nephrology.metaDescription: Nephrology analytics that account for dialysis schedules, rounding days and CKD follow-up volume. See the clinic metrics in a 15-minute demo.
analytics/nephrology.h1: Nephrology Analytics Built Around Dialysis Schedules and CKD Clinics
analytics/nephrology.subtitle: clinIQ shows how dialysis shifts, unit rounding and CKD follow-up volume shape your clinic days, so you can schedule against real patterns.
analytics/nephrology.problemHeading: Clinic Days Compete with Dialysis Days
analytics/nephrology.problemStatement: Nephrology clinics serve patients whose week is already booked. In-center hemodialysis patients are tied to a Monday-Wednesday-Friday or Tuesday-Thursday-Saturday shift, and an office visit on a dialysis day often turns into a cancellation. Nephrologists round at dialysis units, so clinic sessions on rounding days start late. Meanwhile CKD follow-ups, new referrals and transplant evaluations all need different visit lengths. Most practices know these pressures exist but cannot see how much each one costs them in access and missed visits.
analytics/nephrology.solutionHeading: Clinic Metrics That Reflect How Nephrology Works
analytics/nephrology.solutionStatement: clinIQ Analytics breaks no-shows, late starts and wait times out by day of week, session, provider and visit type. Practices can see whether missed visits cluster on certain weekdays, whether rounding mornings push first appointments back and which visit types run over their slots. Live dashboards show who is waiting and which rooms are open. Historical reports give the manager evidence for rebuilding templates around dialysis shifts and rounding schedules instead of relying on memory.

workflow.h2: How a Nephrology Clinic Session Becomes Data
workflow.intro: clinIQ captures each step of the visit and rolls it into reports your team can act on.

steps.title: Arrival and vitals
steps.body: The patient checks in and moves to rooming, where staff take blood pressure and weight. clinIQ logs arrival and rooming times. Reports show waiting room time by session, which matters when patients who rely on medical transport arrive in clusters or well past their appointment time.

steps.title: Provider start after rounding
steps.body: On rounding days the first patient often waits for the nephrologist to return from the dialysis unit. Analytics tracks first-patient on-time rate by provider and weekday, so the practice can see whether rounding mornings need a later template start or a lighter first hour.

steps.title: Visit and checkout
steps.body: Exam room time is measured by visit type, so new CKD referrals, routine follow-ups and transplant evaluations each get their own average. Schedulers can match slot length to what visits actually take. Our post on [nephrology patient flow and dialysis coordination](/blog/nephrology-patient-flow-dialysis-coordination) covers the scheduling side.

steps.title: Weekly review
steps.body: A scheduled report lands in the manager's inbox each Monday with last week's no-shows by weekday, late starts by provider and visit-type overruns. Trends over several months show whether template changes actually reduced missed visits or simply moved them to another day.

items.title: No-shows by weekday and session
items.body: See whether missed appointments concentrate on specific days or sessions. If they line up with common dialysis shifts, the practice has evidence to steer dialysis patients toward their off days when booking follow-ups.

items.title: First-patient on-time rate
items.body: Track how often each nephrologist starts clinic on time, split by rounding and non-rounding days. Late starts carry through the whole session, so this one metric often explains why afternoon waits run long.

items.title: Visit length by visit type
items.body: Compare scheduled and actual exam time for new referrals, CKD follow-ups and transplant visits. Consistent overruns show which slots need more time and which templates are packed tighter than the work allows.

items.title: RTM program tracking
items.body: For practices running remote monitoring for blood pressure and weight, analytics reports enrollment and monitoring activity alongside clinic metrics in one place. See our guide to [CKD remote monitoring](/blog/ckd-rtm-chronic-kidney-disease-monitoring) for program setup.

faqs.q: What metrics should a nephrology practice track?
faqs.a: Start with no-show rate by weekday, first-patient on-time rate, waiting room time and actual visit length by visit type. Those four show how dialysis schedules, rounding and visit mix affect access. clinIQ reports all of them automatically from check-in and rooming timestamps, then trends them over time so you can measure the effect of schedule changes.

faqs.q: How can we reduce missed visits from dialysis patients?
faqs.a: First confirm the pattern. clinIQ shows no-shows by weekday and session, so you can see whether missed visits line up with dialysis shift days. If they do, schedule those patients on their off days and add reminder outreach for the highest-risk bookings. Then compare the no-show trend before and after the change to confirm it worked.

faqs.q: Does clinIQ track time nephrologists spend rounding at dialysis units?
faqs.a: clinIQ measures clinic operations: arrivals, rooming, provider start times and visit length. It shows the effect of rounding on clinic, such as late first appointments on rounding days, without tracking work done inside the dialysis unit. That effect on clinic is usually the question managers need answered when building or revising templates.

faqs.q: Can providers see their own clinic metrics?
faqs.a: Yes. Each nephrologist can see their queue in real time and review their own visit length, schedule adherence and on-time starts over any period. Data framed this way supports practical conversations about templates and session design, because everyone is looking at the same numbers rather than competing impressions of a hard day.

analytics/ophthalmology.problemHeading: Long Eye Visits With No Clear Cause
analytics/ophthalmology.problemStatement: An ophthalmology visit is several visits in one. The patient checks in, goes through technician workup, gets dilated, waits for the drops to work, moves to OCT or visual fields, then sees the doctor. Retina injection days and post-op cataract checks add their own queues. Patients complain about being in the building for hours, but the practice cannot tell which segment is the problem. Adding a technician, a scribe or an imaging slot is a guess without that breakdown.
analytics/ophthalmology.solutionHeading: Segment-Level Reporting for Every Eye Visit
analytics/ophthalmology.solutionStatement: clinIQ records a timestamp at each status change: checked in, in workup, dilating, in testing, ready for doctor, with doctor, checkout. Analytics reports the time spent in each segment by day, doctor, technician and visit type. The live dashboard shows which patients are dilated and ready, so the doctor's next patient is never a mystery. Over weeks, reports reveal whether imaging, workup capacity or doctor pacing drives total visit time, and changes can be measured against a baseline.

workflow.h2: How an Eye Clinic Visit Is Measured in clinIQ
workflow.intro: Each handoff becomes a measured segment, so total visit time can be explained step by step.

steps.title: Check-in to workup
steps.body: clinIQ logs arrival and the moment a technician takes the patient back. Waiting room time by hour shows when workup capacity falls behind arrivals, which is common in the first hour of a busy clinic and again right after lunch when afternoon patients arrive together.

steps.title: Workup and dilation
steps.body: Technician workup time is measured per technician and visit type. Dilation status is visible on the live board with a running timer, and reports show how long dilated patients wait beyond the time drops need to take effect before anyone moves them forward.

steps.title: Diagnostic testing
steps.body: OCT, visual fields and photography are tracked as their own segment. Reports show testing queue time by device and hour, so you know when imaging is the bottleneck. Our post on the [ophthalmology diagnostic testing workflow](/blog/ophthalmology-diagnostic-testing-workflow) goes deeper into ordering and sequencing.

steps.title: Doctor exam and checkout
steps.body: Time from ready-for-doctor to doctor entry measures doctor pacing. Doctor time per visit type and patients seen per session roll into provider reports. Checkout time closes the visit, completes the total and shows whether the front desk adds a final wait.

items.title: Visit segment breakdown
items.body: One report shows waiting, workup, dilation, testing and doctor time stacked for each visit type. It answers where the hours go without a manual time study, and it updates every day the clinic runs.

items.title: Technician productivity
items.body: See workups completed per technician per session and average workup time by visit type. Comparing like with like supports fair staffing decisions and shows where newer technicians need more training.

items.title: Imaging queue reports
items.body: Track waits for OCT, visual fields and other testing by hour of day. When testing backs up, the data shows whether to add a device slot, move a technician to imaging or change visit ordering.

items.title: Injection and post-op day reporting
items.body: Filter reports to retina injection clinics or post-op cataract days, which run on different rhythms than comprehensive exams. Each clinic type gets measured on its own terms instead of being averaged together.

faqs.q: Why do eye exams take so long?
faqs.a: A full ophthalmology visit includes check-in, technician workup, dilation, diagnostic testing and the doctor exam. Waits can build at any of those steps, and drops alone need time to work. clinIQ measures each segment separately, so a practice can see whether patients mostly wait for workup, imaging or the doctor, then fix the step that adds the most time.

faqs.q: What KPIs should an ophthalmology practice track?
faqs.a: Useful operational KPIs include total visit time, waiting room time, workup time per technician, imaging queue time, ready-for-doctor wait and patients per doctor session. No-show rate by visit type also matters for high-volume clinics. clinIQ reports these from status timestamps, so they reflect what happened in the building rather than what was scheduled.

faqs.q: Can clinIQ show which patients are dilated and ready?
faqs.a: Yes. The live dashboard shows each patient's status, including dilating and ready for doctor, along with how long they have been in that status. Doctors and scribes can see the next ready patient from any screen without walking the hallway or asking the technicians. Patients who have waited too long are highlighted so someone can step in.

faqs.q: Can we track technician performance fairly?
faqs.a: Yes. Reports show workups per session and average time by visit type, so a technician handling complex retina workups is compared with similar work, not with quick post-op checks. The goal is staffing and training decisions backed by data. Managers use it to balance assignments and spot where support is needed, not to rank people.
