check-in/urgent-care.h1: Urgent Care Check-In Built for Walk-In Volume
check-in/urgent-care.subtitle: Patients start check-in from home or at a kiosk by the door, so registration, chief complaint and insurance are done before they reach the desk. Staff spend the surge on triage, not data entry.
check-in/urgent-care.problemHeading: The Urgent Care Front Desk at 6 PM
check-in/urgent-care.problemStatement: Urgent care volume arrives in surges: Monday mornings, the after-work rush, weekends and respiratory season. Every walk-in needs identity, insurance, history and chief complaint captured from scratch. When three people arrive at once, a line forms at the desk while rooms sit empty. Patients standing in that line can't tell how long the wait will be, and some leave before they're seen. Paper registration also slows triage, because the nurse can't see who has chest pain or trouble breathing until the clipboard comes back.
check-in/urgent-care.solutionHeading: Move Registration Off the Desk and Ahead of Arrival
check-in/urgent-care.solutionStatement: With clinIQ, patients check in online before they leave home and hold their place in the queue while they travel. Walk-ins use a kiosk near the entrance that scans a driver's license, photographs the insurance card, collects the reason for visit and takes the copay. Each completed check-in appears on the [patient flow board](/features/patient-flow) with the chief complaint, so the triage nurse sees who needs attention first. Front desk staff handle only flagged exceptions, such as insurance that won't verify or a workers' comp visit that needs employer details.

workflow.h2: How a Walk-In Moves Through clinIQ Check-In
workflow.intro: Whether the patient starts on a phone at home or at the kiosk in your lobby, the record they create is the same.

steps.title: Online check-in from home
steps.body: The patient picks your location and starts check-in on their phone. They enter demographics, reason for visit and insurance, then see their place in the queue. They arrive closer to their turn instead of spending the wait in your lobby, which keeps seats open during a surge.

steps.title: Kiosk for walk-ins
steps.body: Patients who didn't check in online use the kiosk at the entrance. They scan a driver's license or type their name and date of birth, photograph the front and back of the insurance card, answer the intake questions and pay the copay by card. Then they sit down.

steps.title: Triage sees the chief complaint
steps.body: Completed check-ins land on the board with arrival time and reason for visit. The triage nurse can pull a patient with shortness of breath ahead of a sprained ankle, and the queue reflects acuity instead of arrival order alone. Nobody waits on a clipboard to learn who is sick.

steps.title: Front desk works exceptions
steps.body: Alerts tell staff exactly what needs a person: an insurance card that won't verify, a self-pay patient asking about price, a minor without a signed guardian consent, or a work injury that needs employer and claim details. Everyone else moves straight to rooming.

items.title: Place-in-line online check-in
items.body: Patients join the queue from home and track their place on the way in. Arrivals spread out across the hour, and the lobby doesn't fill up the moment a surge starts.

items.title: License and insurance card capture
items.body: Kiosk and phone check-in scan driver's licenses and photograph insurance cards, cutting the typing errors that turn into denied claims weeks later. Eligibility is checked during check-in, not after the visit.

items.title: Copay and self-pay at arrival
items.body: Patients see their copay or self-pay amount and pay by card during check-in. Collection no longer depends on catching them at discharge, when they are in a hurry to reach the pharmacy.

items.title: Occupational medicine intake
items.body: Workers' comp and employer-paid visits can use their own intake forms for employer, claim and injury details, so those visits are billed to the right party the first time. Employer billing questions are settled at the door.

items.title: Wait status in the lobby
items.body: Pair check-in with [LobbyView](/features/lobbyview) so waiting patients see where they stand on a lobby screen without names, which cuts the "how much longer" questions at the desk. Patients who can see the line moving are less likely to walk out.

faqs.q: How does online check-in work for urgent care?
faqs.a: The patient starts check-in on their phone before leaving home, entering demographics, insurance and reason for visit. They get a place in the queue and arrive closer to when a room is likely to open. It isn't a fixed appointment, because acuity still decides the order, but it moves registration out of the lobby and spreads out arrivals during busy hours.

faqs.q: Should an urgent care use kiosk check-in or phone check-in?
faqs.a: Most centers need both. Phone check-in from home serves patients who plan ahead and reduces lobby crowding. A kiosk near the entrance handles walk-ins who arrive without checking in, including patients who would rather not use their own phone. Staff stay available for anyone who struggles with either. Our comparison of [kiosk and phone check-in for urgent care](/blog/urgent-care-check-in-kiosk-phone) goes deeper.

faqs.q: Does online check-in reduce patients leaving without being seen?
faqs.a: It addresses the main cause, which is uncertainty. Patients who check in from home spend less time in the lobby, and patients who can see their place in line are less likely to assume they were forgotten. Keeping walkouts down also depends on rooming and provider throughput, which is why check-in feeds directly into patient flow tracking.

faqs.q: Can patients pay their copay at an urgent care kiosk?
faqs.a: Yes. After the patient confirms their information, the kiosk shows the copay or self-pay amount and accepts card payment. Phone and web check-in offer the same option. Collecting at check-in means payment doesn't depend on catching the patient at discharge, when they are often in a hurry to fill a prescription and get home.

scheduling/occupational-therapy.h1: Occupational Therapy Scheduling Around the Plan of Care
scheduling/occupational-therapy.subtitle: clinIQ books OT visits as a recurring series matched to the plan of care, keeps patients with the right therapist and fills open slots before they cost the day.
scheduling/occupational-therapy.problemHeading: Why OT Schedules Are So Hard to Keep Full
scheduling/occupational-therapy.problemStatement: Occupational therapy runs on recurring visits: two or three a week for several weeks under a plan of care. Each patient needs a therapist with the right skills, whether hand therapy and splint fabrication, neuro rehab or pediatric sensory work. Pediatric patients often can only come after school, so late afternoons overflow while mornings sit open. Missed visits slow progress, and payer visit limits and Medicare progress report and recertification timing add rules the front desk has to remember.
scheduling/occupational-therapy.solutionHeading: Recurring OT Scheduling That Follows the Plan
scheduling/occupational-therapy.solutionStatement: clinIQ books the plan of care as a series at the frequency the therapist sets, on consistent days and times. Templates separate evaluations, treatment visits and splint fabrication by length and therapist skill. Staff can see visits used against the plan, so re-evaluations and progress reports are booked before they are due. When a patient cancels, the waitlist offers the slot to another patient who wants more visits or a better time.

workflow.h2: How an OT Episode Moves Through clinIQ Scheduling
workflow.intro: The evaluation sets the plan, and the schedule carries it through to discharge.

steps.title: Evaluation booked
steps.body: The scheduler books the evaluation template, which blocks a longer visit with a therapist whose skills match the referral. A hand therapy referral goes to a certified hand therapist if the clinic has one. A pediatric referral goes to a pediatric therapist in an after-school slot.

steps.title: Series set from the plan
steps.body: After the evaluation, the plan of care frequency becomes a recurring series, such as twice a week for six weeks. Patients get consistent times, which helps attendance. The series is managed as a group, so a schedule change updates every remaining visit at once.

steps.title: Milestones on the calendar
steps.body: Re-evaluations and progress visits are booked at the points your documentation rules require. Staff see visits used against the plan and any payer limit, and can work with our [visit cap tracking guide](/blog/pt-visit-cap-tracking) to keep authorization ahead of the schedule.

steps.title: Gaps filled
steps.body: When a patient cancels, the waitlist texts matching patients who asked for more sessions or a different time. A yes reply books the slot, and no reply moves the offer to the next patient. Therapists keep a full day, and patients who want to progress faster can.

items.title: Therapist skill matching
items.body: Templates specify which therapists can see each visit type, such as hand therapy, splinting, neuro rehab or pediatrics. Schedulers see only qualified therapists with open time, so a patient is not booked with the wrong clinician.

items.title: Space and equipment rules
items.body: Splint fabrication, sensory gym sessions and ADL kitchen training can reserve the room or equipment they need. Two sessions do not compete for the same space, and setup time is built into the template.

items.title: After-school demand
items.body: Analytics show where pediatric demand stacks up after school, so leadership can shift therapist hours or add late sessions instead of letting a waitlist grow while morning slots stay open.

items.title: No-show patterns
items.body: Attendance by patient, day and time shows who is drifting from the plan of care. Overbooking rules can cover short treatment visits in high-risk slots without overloading the therapist when everyone arrives.

items.title: Multi-location schedules
items.body: Clinics with several sites keep location-specific rooms, therapists and rules. Therapists who travel between clinics see one combined schedule, and analytics can report by site or across the whole organization.

faqs.q: What is the best way to schedule recurring occupational therapy visits?
faqs.a: Book the plan of care as a series right after the evaluation, at the set frequency and on consistent days and times. Patients with a fixed routine attend more reliably than those booked one visit at a time. clinIQ creates the series in one step and lets staff move it as a group if the patient's availability changes.

faqs.q: How can an OT clinic reduce cancellations and no-shows?
faqs.a: Use reminders, consistent visit times and an easy way to reschedule instead of skipping. Track attendance by patient so therapists can address drop-off early. clinIQ adds waitlist automation, which fills a canceled slot by text with a patient who wants it. Our article on [reducing no-shows through scheduling](/blog/no-show-reduction-scheduling) covers the tactics in more detail.

faqs.q: Can clinIQ help with Medicare progress report and recertification timing?
faqs.a: Yes, on the scheduling side. Staff can book progress visits and re-evaluations at the points your documentation rules require and see visits used against the plan of care. clinIQ does not write the clinical documentation. It makes sure the visit where that work happens is on the calendar in time.

faqs.q: Can pediatric and adult OT share one schedule?
faqs.a: Yes. Each visit type has its own template with length, therapist skill and space requirements. Pediatric sessions can be weighted toward after-school hours while adult and hand therapy visits fill the morning, all on one schedule. Analytics then show whether the split matches real demand at each hour. Staff can then adjust therapist hours.

analytics/radiology.metaDescription: Report scanner utilization, check-in-to-scan time and no-shows by modality for outpatient imaging. See the radiology dashboards in a demo.
analytics/radiology.h1: Radiology Analytics for Scanner Utilization and Check-In-to-Scan Time
analytics/radiology.subtitle: clinIQ measures each outpatient imaging visit from arrival to exam completion, by modality, so you can protect scanner time and shorten patient waits.
analytics/radiology.problemStatement: An outpatient imaging center lives on scanner time. MRI, CT, ultrasound and mammography each run on different exam lengths and prep requirements. A patient who arrives without completed MRI safety screening, a missing kidney function result before contrast, or an authorization that is not approved can leave a slot empty. Walk-in X-ray patients stack up at the same hours as scheduled exams. Most centers can report exam volume, but not how long patients waited, how long rooms sat idle or why slots went unused.
analytics/radiology.solutionStatement: clinIQ timestamps arrival, screening complete, prep complete, in room and exam complete. Analytics turns those into check-in-to-scan time, room utilization and exam duration by modality, protocol type and hour. No-shows and same-day cancellations are reported by modality and lead time. The live dashboard shows which rooms are open and which patients are waiting on prep. Leadership gets evidence for where to add a technologist shift, extend hours or tighten pre-visit screening.

workflow.h2: How an Imaging Visit Is Measured in clinIQ
workflow.intro: Every step from the front desk to the scanner table is timed and reported by modality.

steps.title: Arrival and screening
steps.body: The patient checks in and completes screening forms, such as the MRI safety questionnaire, on their phone or at the desk. clinIQ logs when screening is done. Reports show how often screening delays the exam and at which hours and modalities it happens most.

steps.title: Prep and changing
steps.body: Contrast prep, IV placement and changing are tracked as their own segment. Analytics shows prep time by modality and flags patients waiting past your threshold, so a technologist or nurse can step in before the scanner room goes idle and the schedule slips.

steps.title: In room and exam complete
steps.body: Room-in and exam-complete times feed utilization and exam duration reports. Compare actual duration with the scheduled slot for each protocol type to see which exams are booked too short, which are booked too long and where the template is leaving time on the table.

steps.title: Unused slots review
steps.body: No-shows, late arrivals and same-day cancellations are reported by modality, weekday and lead time. Slots lost to pending approvals point back to the authorization process, which [clinIQ pre-authorization tracking](/features/pre-auth) handles well before the patient is ever placed on the schedule.

items.title: Room utilization by modality
items.body: See what share of operating hours each MRI, CT, ultrasound or mammography room had a patient on the table. Idle stretches show up by hour and weekday, which points to where extended hours or schedule changes would pay off.

items.title: Check-in-to-scan time
items.body: Track the full wait from arrival to room entry, split into screening, prep and queue time. This is the number patients feel most, and the report shows exactly which part of it to fix first.

items.title: Exam duration versus slot
items.body: Compare booked slot length with actual exam time by modality and protocol type. Templates can then match how long exams really take, which protects both throughput and technologist workload across the day.

items.title: No-show and lead time analysis
items.body: Report no-shows by modality and by days between booking and exam. Long lead times often predict missed exams, so this report helps target reminder outreach and decide how far out each modality should book.

faqs.q: How do you measure MRI or CT scanner utilization?
faqs.a: Compare the time a patient is actually in the room against the hours the scanner is staffed and available. clinIQ uses room-in and exam-complete timestamps rather than the schedule, so the report reflects real use. Breaking it out by hour and weekday shows whether idle time comes from late starts, prep delays, no-shows or slots that were never booked.

faqs.q: What metrics matter most for an outpatient imaging center?
faqs.a: Room utilization by modality, check-in-to-scan time, exam duration versus scheduled slot, no-show rate by modality and same-day cancellations are the core operational set. Walk-in wait time matters too if you offer X-ray without appointments. clinIQ reports each one automatically and trends them weekly or monthly so you can measure the effect of changes.

faqs.q: Can clinIQ show why imaging slots go unused?
faqs.a: Yes. Unused slots are reported by cause where staff record it, such as no-show, late arrival, incomplete screening or authorization not ready. Seeing the causes side by side shows whether to focus on reminders, pre-visit screening or authorization follow-up first, and later reports confirm whether the fix reduced lost slots.

faqs.q: Does clinIQ replace our RIS reporting?
faqs.a: No. Your RIS and PACS manage orders, images and reads. clinIQ covers the operational side of the visit: where patients are, how long they wait at each step and how rooms are used across the day. The two systems answer different questions, and imaging leaders typically need both views to manage capacity well.

patient-flow/dentistry.metaDescription: See which operatories are seated, which hygiene patients need the doctor's exam and which rooms are in turnover. Keep a dental office on time. Book a demo.
patient-flow/dentistry.h1: Dental Patient Flow and Operatory Tracking Software
patient-flow/dentistry.subtitle: A live view of every operatory, hygiene chair and patient, so the dentist knows which hygiene exam is next and the front desk knows why the schedule is slipping.
patient-flow/dentistry.problemHeading: Where a Dental Schedule Loses Time
patient-flow/dentistry.problemStatement: A dental office runs the doctor's column and several hygiene columns at once, and they depend on each other. Hygienists wait for the dentist to come in for the periodic exam. The dentist moves between a crown prep, a filling where the anesthetic is still taking effect and two hygiene checks. Assistants turn over operatories while instruments cycle through sterilization. Emergency patients with tooth pain get squeezed in. When no one can see the whole floor, the doctor's next move is decided by whoever catches them in the hallway.
patient-flow/dentistry.solutionHeading: Every Operatory and Every Handoff on One Screen
patient-flow/dentistry.solutionStatement: clinIQ tracks each patient from check-in to checkout and each operatory as available, occupied, in turnover or blocked. Hygienists tap a status when a patient is ready for the doctor's exam, and that request appears in the dentist's queue with the operatory number and how long it has waited. Assistants mark rooms ready after turnover. The front desk sees arrivals, seated patients and who is running behind, and can give a waiting patient an honest answer about timing.

workflow.h2: How a Dental Visit Moves Through clinIQ
workflow.intro: A recall hygiene visit and a restorative appointment, running side by side.

steps.title: Check-in and seating
steps.body: The patient checks in on their phone or at the desk and joins the queue for their hygienist or the doctor's column. When an assistant or hygienist seats them, the operatory flips to occupied with the provider attached, so the front desk can see the patient is in the chair.

steps.title: Doctor's exam requested
steps.body: Near the end of the cleaning, the hygienist taps that the patient is ready for the exam. The dentist's queue shows the request, the operatory and the time waiting. Hygienists stop stepping into the hall or sending an assistant to find the doctor.

steps.title: Doctor moves between operatories
steps.body: While anesthetic takes effect in one chair, the dentist checks the queue and goes to the hygiene exam that has waited longest. The board shows every patient's status, so the doctor's time goes where it is needed next instead of to whoever asked first.

steps.title: Checkout and turnover
steps.body: When the patient heads to checkout and scheduling, the operatory moves to turnover. The assistant wipes down, sets up for the next procedure and marks the room ready. The turnover timer shows when a room is stuck, often because instruments are still in sterilization.

items.title: Operatory status board
items.body: Each operatory, including hygiene rooms and any dedicated imaging space, shows whether it is available, occupied, in turnover or blocked for an equipment problem. Staff stop walking the floor to find an open chair.

items.title: Hygiene exam queue
items.body: The dentist sees every pending hygiene exam in one list, sorted by wait time. Hygienists aren't left holding a finished patient while the next one sits in reception and the schedule slides.

items.title: Every column in one view
items.body: One view covers the doctor's column and every hygiene column, so the office manager sees where the day is slipping across all providers. See how this works in [multi-provider practices](/blog/patient-flow-multi-provider-practices).

items.title: Emergency patient fit-ins
items.body: When a patient with tooth pain walks in, the front desk can see which operatory opens next and which provider has a gap, instead of guessing and interrupting the doctor mid-procedure.

items.title: Wait time by segment
items.body: Wait time is split into reception wait and chair wait before the provider arrives. That shows whether delays come from seating, turnover or the doctor's pace, by provider and by day.

faqs.q: How do dentists keep hygiene exams from backing up?
faqs.a: Give the dentist a single queue of pending exams. In clinIQ, the hygienist taps when the patient is ready, and the request shows in the dentist's queue with the operatory number and wait time. The dentist picks up the longest wait between procedures instead of relying on hallway signals, and the office can see how long hygienists typically wait.

faqs.q: What is operatory tracking software?
faqs.a: It is a live view of every treatment room in a dental office, showing which operatories are seated, which are being turned over and which are free. clinIQ adds patient status to that view, so staff see who is waiting in reception, who is in the chair and who is ready for the doctor, without walking the floor.

faqs.q: Does patient flow software replace our dental practice management system?
faqs.a: No. clinIQ sits on top of the system you already use for charting, scheduling and billing. It adds the real-time layer those systems usually lack: where each patient is right now, which rooms are ready and who is waiting on whom. Appointment data comes from your existing system, so staff don't enter it twice.

faqs.q: How do you reduce patient wait times in a dental office?
faqs.a: Start by measuring where the wait happens. Time in reception points to seating or turnover delays. Time in the chair before the doctor arrives points to exam handoffs or an overbooked doctor column. clinIQ tracks both segments by provider and day, so changes to the template, such as more buffer for exams, are based on real data.

analytics/gastroenterology.metaDescription: Track endoscopy room turnover, first-case starts and prep-related cancellations alongside GI clinic flow. See the reports in a 15-minute demo.
analytics/gastroenterology.h1: Gastroenterology Analytics for Endoscopy Turnover and Clinic Flow
analytics/gastroenterology.subtitle: clinIQ measures procedure rooms, pre-op and recovery bays along with office visits, so GI practices can see where procedure days and clinic days lose time.
analytics/gastroenterology.problemHeading: Procedure Days Run on Tight Margins
analytics/gastroenterology.problemStatement: A GI endoscopy day depends on a chain: the patient arrives on time with a driver, pre-op is complete, the room is turned over, anesthesia is ready and recovery bays have space. When the first case starts late, every colonoscopy after it slides. Same-day cancellations for inadequate bowel prep or no ride leave holes that are hard to fill. Clinic days have their own pressures, with new consults and follow-ups competing for slots. Most practices sense these losses but do not measure them.
analytics/gastroenterology.solutionStatement: clinIQ timestamps arrival, pre-op complete, in room, procedure end, room ready and recovery discharge. Analytics reports first-case on-time starts, room turnover time, pre-op wait and recovery bay time by room, day and physician. Same-day cancellations are tracked by reason, so prep failures and missing drivers show up as patterns. The same module reports clinic wait times and visit length, giving GI leadership one view across the office and the endoscopy suite.

workflow.h2: How an Endoscopy Day Is Measured in clinIQ
workflow.intro: Each status change in the procedure unit becomes part of a report.

steps.title: Arrival and pre-op
steps.body: The patient checks in and moves to a pre-op bay for history, consent and IV placement. clinIQ logs arrival and pre-op complete. Reports show pre-op wait by hour and flag the mornings where arrivals outpace nursing capacity and push the first case back.

steps.title: First case and room time
steps.body: First-case start is compared with the scheduled time for each room and physician. In-room and procedure-end times feed room utilization reports. See our guide to [colonoscopy and EGD scheduling](/blog/gi-procedure-scheduling-colonoscopy-egd) for how to design room templates and case order around those numbers.

steps.title: Turnover
steps.body: The gap between one patient leaving and the next entering is room turnover. clinIQ reports it by room, day and time of day, and live alerts flag rooms in turnover past your threshold so staff can respond while the delay is still small.

steps.title: Recovery and discharge
steps.body: Recovery bay time is tracked through discharge to the driver. When bays fill, patients stay in procedure rooms and the next case waits. Reports show whether recovery capacity, not the procedure room, is the real limit on how many cases the unit can run.

items.title: First-case on-time rate
items.body: Track how often the first procedure in each room starts on time, by physician and weekday. Late first cases are often the main reason the whole endoscopy day runs over, so this is usually the first metric to fix.

items.title: Room turnover time
items.body: See average and outlier turnover by room and hour. Trend it weekly to confirm whether a new cleaning, scope handling or room setup routine actually shortened the gap between cases.

items.title: Same-day cancellation reasons
items.body: Report cancellations by reason, such as inadequate prep, no driver or no-show, and by lead time. Patterns point to the right fix, whether clearer prep instructions, a confirmation call or a different booking window.

items.title: Clinic visit metrics
items.body: Report waiting room time, visit length by type and no-shows for office days. Consult access and procedure capacity can then be planned together, since today's new consult is next month's colonoscopy.

faqs.q: How do you measure endoscopy room turnover?
faqs.a: Measure from the time one patient leaves the procedure room to the time the next patient enters. clinIQ records both events automatically and reports turnover by room, physician and time of day. Outliers are easy to spot, and trending the average over weeks shows whether process changes such as parallel setup or added techs actually worked.

faqs.q: What KPIs should a GI practice track?
faqs.a: For procedure days: first-case on-time rate, room utilization, turnover time, pre-op wait, recovery time and same-day cancellations by reason. For clinic days: waiting room time, visit length by type and no-show rate. clinIQ reports all of these from status timestamps and lets you view the office and endoscopy unit separately or together.

faqs.q: Can clinIQ track colonoscopy cancellations from poor bowel prep?
faqs.a: Yes, when staff record the cancellation reason. Analytics then reports prep-related cancellations by weekday, physician and lead time, and by prep instruction set if you track which one each patient received. That shows whether prep education, appointment timing, day-before calls or reminder outreach needs the most attention from your team.

faqs.q: Does clinIQ work for an endoscopy center and an office together?
faqs.a: Yes. Reports can be filtered by location, so a GI group can see endoscopy unit metrics and office metrics separately or combined. Multi-site groups can compare units side by side to find which ones turn rooms fastest or start on time most often, and use that as the model for other sites.

analytics/orthodontics.metaTitle: Orthodontic Practice Analytics and Chair Reports
analytics/orthodontics.metaDescription: Track chair utilization, doctor-check wait times and missed adjustment visits in your orthodontic practice. See the reports in a short demo.
analytics/orthodontics.h1: Orthodontic Analytics for Chair Time, Doctor Checks and Missed Visits
analytics/orthodontics.subtitle: clinIQ shows how your open bay actually runs, from the after-school rush to emergency visits, so you can schedule chairs and assistants with confidence.
analytics/orthodontics.problemHeading: The After-School Rush Hides Lost Chair Time
analytics/orthodontics.problemStatement: Orthodontic schedules are lopsided. Families want the late-afternoon slots, so chairs fill after school and sit lighter in the morning. Assistants finish adjustments and wait for the doctor check while the next patient waits in the reception area. Broken brackets and poking wires get squeezed in as emergency visits. Missed adjustment appointments can extend treatment and push debond dates. Most practices can count patients seen, but not how long chairs sit idle or how long assistants wait on the doctor.
analytics/orthodontics.solutionHeading: Chair and Doctor-Check Metrics for the Open Bay
analytics/orthodontics.solutionStatement: clinIQ records when each patient is seated, when the assistant is ready for the doctor, when the doctor check happens and when the chair is released. Analytics reports chair utilization by hour, doctor-check wait time, appointment length by type and missed visits by day and time. The live view shows which chairs are waiting for the doctor right now. Reports help you rebalance templates, assistant coverage and emergency slots based on what really happens in the bay.

workflow.h2: How an Adjustment Visit Is Measured in clinIQ
workflow.intro: A routine visit becomes a set of timed steps that roll into chair and doctor reports.

steps.title: Check-in
steps.body: The patient or parent checks in on their phone or at the desk, and clinIQ starts the clock. Reception wait time is reported by hour, which shows how much the late-afternoon peak stretches waits compared with morning slots and where families are waiting longest.

steps.title: Seated with assistant
steps.body: When an assistant seats the patient, clinIQ logs the chair and the time. Assistant time per appointment type, such as wire change, aligner check, bonding or debond, is reported over time so templates match the real work each visit takes.

steps.title: Doctor check
steps.body: The assistant flags the patient as ready for the doctor. clinIQ measures the wait until the doctor arrives at the chair. This doctor-check queue is often the hidden reason the bay backs up, and the live board shows it as it builds.

steps.title: Release and next visit
steps.body: Chair release time completes the visit and feeds utilization reports. Missed and rescheduled adjustment visits are reported by day, time and lead time, helping the treatment coordinator spot patients whose treatment may be slipping before planned debond dates have to move.

items.title: Chair utilization by hour
items.body: See how full each chair is across the day. Morning gaps and after-school overload become clear, which supports decisions like offering morning slots for adults and aligner patients or shifting assistant hours later.

items.title: Doctor-check wait time
items.body: Track the time between ready-for-doctor and the doctor check, by hour and day. It is a direct measure of whether the doctor's chair rotation keeps up with the number of assistants running chairs at once.

items.title: Missed visit tracking
items.body: Report missed and late-canceled adjustment visits by weekday, time slot and lead time, with a patient-level list your coordinator can use for follow-up calls. Read about common patterns in our post on [no-show analytics](/blog/no-show-analytics-patterns).

items.title: Emergency visit load
items.body: See how many emergency visits for broken brackets or loose wires land each day and when. If they cluster at certain times, a dedicated emergency block may protect the regular schedule from constant squeeze-ins.

faqs.q: What KPIs should an orthodontic practice track?
faqs.a: For daily operations: chair utilization by hour, reception wait time, doctor-check wait, appointment length by type, missed visit rate and emergency visit volume. clinIQ reports each one from check-in and chair timestamps, then trends them so you can see whether template or staffing changes help. Multi-office groups can compare these numbers by location.

faqs.q: How do you reduce doctor-check wait times in an open bay?
faqs.a: Measure it first. clinIQ shows how long assistants wait for the doctor by hour, so you can see whether waits spike at peak times. Common fixes include adjusting how many chairs run per doctor at peak, staggering appointment starts by a few minutes and adding a second doctor block on the heaviest afternoons.

faqs.q: Can clinIQ show which patients keep missing adjustments?
faqs.a: Yes. Patient-level reports list repeated missed or rescheduled visits along with the time since the last completed adjustment. Because the list updates automatically, the treatment coordinator can work through it each week and reach out to families before treatment time stretches further and planned debond dates have to move later.

faqs.q: Does analytics help with the after-school rush?
faqs.a: Yes. Reports show arrivals, waits and chair use by hour, so you can see exactly how the late-afternoon peak compares with the rest of the day. Practices use that data to move suitable visit types to mornings, set assistant schedules and decide how many chairs and assistants to run at peak.

scheduling/vestibular-therapy.metaDescription: Vestibular rehab scheduling that sizes evaluations, books VNG testing with prep reminders and keeps BPPV patients seen quickly. See it with your clinic.
scheduling/vestibular-therapy.h1: Vestibular Therapy Scheduling for Dizziness and Balance Care
scheduling/vestibular-therapy.subtitle: clinIQ books vestibular evaluations, repositioning visits, VNG testing and rehab series on templates that fit how dizzy patients are actually seen.
scheduling/vestibular-therapy.problemHeading: Why Vestibular Schedules Need Different Rules
scheduling/vestibular-therapy.problemStatement: Vestibular patients do not fit a standard therapy grid. A full evaluation with positional testing takes longer than a routine visit. A patient with BPPV may need only a repositioning maneuver and a recheck, and a fast appointment matters because symptoms are disabling. VNG testing needs the equipment, a trained clinician and patients who have held vestibular suppressants as instructed. Many patients cannot drive while dizzy, so they depend on a ride and cancel when it falls through.
scheduling/vestibular-therapy.solutionStatement: clinIQ gives each vestibular visit type its own length, clinician and equipment rules. Evaluations get a long block, repositioning rechecks a short one, and VNG testing reserves the testing room and system. Same-day capacity is held for acute dizziness referrals. Reminders reach patients early enough to follow testing prep and arrange a ride. When a visit cancels, the waitlist fills it with another patient who wants to be seen sooner.

workflow.h2: How a Dizziness Referral Moves Through clinIQ
workflow.intro: Referrals from ENT, neurology, audiology or primary care become the right visit with the right clinician.

steps.title: Referral sorted
steps.body: The scheduler chooses the template that fits the referral. Suspected BPPV goes to a prompt evaluation with a vestibular-trained therapist. A complex case with suspected central or bilateral loss gets a longer evaluation, and the provider may add testing. Neither is booked into a generic therapy slot.

steps.title: Testing booked
steps.body: VNG and related testing book on a template that reserves the testing room, the equipment and the clinician. Reminders go out ahead of the test with the practice's prep instructions, including any medication holds, so the test is not wasted on a patient who could not follow prep.

steps.title: Treatment plan scheduled
steps.body: BPPV patients get a short recheck after repositioning to confirm the symptoms have resolved. Patients in vestibular rehab get a recurring series, often weekly, with home exercises between visits. The series is managed as a group, so a change in the plan takes one step.

steps.title: Cancellations refilled
steps.body: When a patient cancels because they have no ride, the [waitlist](/features/scheduling) texts another patient who wants an earlier visit. A yes reply books it without a phone call. The therapist's time is used, and the next dizzy patient is seen sooner.

items.title: Clinician qualification rules
items.body: Vestibular visits are limited to therapists trained in vestibular assessment and canalith repositioning. A patient is never booked with someone who cannot treat them, even when that therapist has open time.

items.title: Equipment reservation
items.body: VNG, rotary chair or balance testing templates reserve the system, the room and the clinician who runs it. Setup and cleanup are built in, so testing does not run into the next patient's visit.

items.title: Held acute capacity
items.body: A small amount of capacity is held each day for new acute dizziness and released on rules if it goes unused. Urgent referrals from the emergency department or primary care do not wait weeks.

items.title: Visit length analytics
items.body: Scheduled and actual times are compared by visit type. If evaluations routinely run over, leadership sees it and resizes the template. Our guide to [appointment templates by visit duration](/blog/appointment-templates-duration) explains the method.

faqs.q: How quickly should a BPPV patient be seen?
faqs.a: As soon as practical. BPPV is usually treatable with repositioning maneuvers, and symptoms can stop patients from working or driving. Holding a small amount of capacity for acute dizziness referrals lets a clinic see them within days rather than adding them to a long queue. clinIQ holds that capacity on rules and releases it if it goes unused.

faqs.q: How long is a vestibular therapy evaluation?
faqs.a: A full vestibular evaluation with history, oculomotor and positional testing and balance assessment usually takes longer than a routine therapy visit. The exact length depends on your clinicians and patient mix. clinIQ lets you set a template for it and compares scheduled time with actual time so you can adjust.

faqs.q: How do clinics help patients prepare for VNG testing?
faqs.a: Patients often need to avoid certain medications, such as vestibular suppressants, and follow other prep before the test, as directed by the ordering clinician. Sending those instructions early enough matters. clinIQ sends reminders with your practice's prep instructions ahead of the test date and lets patients reschedule if they cannot comply.

faqs.q: Can clinIQ coordinate vestibular care with ENT or audiology?
faqs.a: Yes. Multi-department clinics can keep vestibular therapy, ENT and audiology on separate schedules with their own rules while staff book related visits for the same patient in one place. That makes it easier to place testing and therapy on the same day, which matters when the patient needs a ride to every visit.

analytics/chiropractic.metaDescription: Track visits per hour, table turnover, care plan completion and visit caps in your chiropractic clinic. See the dashboards in a 15-minute demo.
analytics/chiropractic.h1: Chiropractic Analytics for Visits per Hour and Care Plan Completion
analytics/chiropractic.subtitle: clinIQ shows how a high-volume chiropractic day really runs and which patients are falling off their care plans, so you can act before visits are lost.
analytics/chiropractic.problemStatement: Chiropractic clinics run short visits at high volume, with peaks before work, at lunch and after work. A few minutes lost per table turn adds up fast across a busy day. New patient exams take much longer than adjustments and can stall the schedule if they land at peak. Patients drop off care plans quietly, and payer visit limits can run out before anyone notices. Most clinics track total visits, but not table turnover, peak-hour waits or plan completion.
analytics/chiropractic.solutionHeading: Volume, Flow and Care Plan Metrics in One Place
analytics/chiropractic.solutionStatement: clinIQ records check-in, room or table assignment, doctor in and checkout for every visit. Analytics reports visits per hour per chiropractor, table turnover, wait times by hour and visit length by type. Care plan reports show visits completed against visits prescribed, and visit cap tracking warns staff as patients near payer limits. Live dashboards show who is waiting and which tables are open, so the front desk can move patients during the rush.

workflow.h2: How a Chiropractic Visit Is Measured in clinIQ
workflow.intro: Short visits still have steps, and each one feeds a report.

steps.title: Check-in
steps.body: The patient checks in by phone or at the desk, and clinIQ starts the visit clock. Waiting room time by hour shows how the early-morning, lunch and after-work peaks stretch waits, and which days of the week the rush is heaviest.

steps.title: Table or room assignment
steps.body: When the patient is placed on a table or in a room, clinIQ logs it. Table turnover time, the gap between one patient leaving and the next arriving, is reported by room and hour, which shows where small delays add up across the day.

steps.title: Adjustment and therapy
steps.body: Doctor-in and doctor-out times show adjustment length, and time in therapy or rehab areas is tracked too. You can see whether the bottleneck is the doctor or the therapy space. Our post on [high-volume chiropractic patient flow](/blog/high-volume-chiropractic-patient-flow) covers floor layout.

steps.title: Checkout and plan tracking
steps.body: At checkout the visit counts toward the patient's care plan and any payer visit limit. Reports list patients who are behind their plan schedule and those nearing their cap, so staff can rebook the patient or request more visits from the payer in time.

items.title: Visits per hour per chiropractor
items.body: See throughput by doctor and hour of day. It shows how close each doctor runs to capacity at peak, where there is room to add visits and when an associate's schedule could absorb overflow.

items.title: Table turnover and utilization
items.body: Track how often each table is occupied and how long it sits empty between patients. Small gains in turnover add real capacity during peak hours without adding space, tables or staff.

items.title: Care plan completion
items.body: Compare visits completed with visits prescribed for each plan. Patients falling behind show up on a follow-up list, so staff can call before the gap turns into a dropped plan.

items.title: Visit cap tracking
items.body: Track visits used against the limits you set for each payer or plan, and flag patients nearing the cap. Read our guide on [chiropractic visit cap tracking](/blog/chiropractic-visit-cap-tracking) for setup details.

faqs.q: What KPIs should a chiropractic clinic track?
faqs.a: Core operational KPIs are visits per hour per chiropractor, wait time by hour, table utilization, care plan completion rate, no-show rate and visits used against payer limits. New patient exam volume matters too. clinIQ reports these automatically from check-in and room timestamps and keeps trends over time, so you can see the effect of every schedule or staffing change.

faqs.q: How do I know when patients are dropping off care plans?
faqs.a: clinIQ compares each patient's completed visits with the visits prescribed in their plan and the expected pace. Patients who fall behind appear on a follow-up list, so staff can reach out before the plan lapses rather than finding out months later when the patient finally returns with the same problem.

faqs.q: Can clinIQ warn us before a patient hits a visit limit?
faqs.a: Yes. Visit cap tracking counts visits against the limit you set for each payer or plan and flags patients as they approach it. That gives staff time to request additional visits, update documentation or discuss self-pay options with the patient before a visit is denied after the fact and becomes a collections problem.

faqs.q: Does analytics help with peak-hour waits?
faqs.a: Yes. Reports show arrivals and waits by hour, and the live board shows open tables in real time. Clinics use that data to adjust staffing for the before-work and after-work rush, move new patient exams to quieter hours and keep the busiest sessions moving without long lobby waits that frustrate regular patients.

scheduling/ophthalmology.metaDescription: Ophthalmology scheduling that accounts for workup, dilation and imaging, keeps anti-VEGF injections on interval and books cataract post-ops. See it live.
scheduling/ophthalmology.h1: Ophthalmology Scheduling for Multi-Step Eye Visits
scheduling/ophthalmology.subtitle: clinIQ books eye visits with the technician workup, dilation, imaging and physician time each one needs, and keeps injection and surgical follow-up intervals on track.
scheduling/ophthalmology.problemHeading: Why Eye Clinic Schedules Run Behind
scheduling/ophthalmology.problemStatement: An ophthalmology visit is several visits in one. A technician takes history, vision and pressure. Many patients are dilated and wait for the drops to work. OCT, visual fields or photos happen at separate stations before the physician sees them. Retina clinics add anti-VEGF injections on intervals of several weeks. Cataract surgery brings pre-op measurements and a set post-op schedule. When every visit gets the same physician slot, the tech and imaging steps back up and the physician waits on them.
scheduling/ophthalmology.solutionStatement: clinIQ builds ophthalmology templates around the whole visit, not just physician time. A dilated exam template accounts for workup and dilation. A glaucoma follow-up with visual fields reserves the field machine. An injection visit is short and books on the patient's interval. Cataract templates book biometry before surgery and the standard post-op visits after it. The schedule spreads imaging-heavy visits across the session so OCT and fields do not become the bottleneck.

workflow.h2: How an Ophthalmology Visit Moves Through clinIQ Scheduling
workflow.intro: Each appointment carries the stations it needs, so the physician's time and the technicians' time both stay realistic.

steps.title: Visit type chosen
steps.body: The scheduler books the template that matches the visit: comprehensive dilated exam, glaucoma follow-up with fields, retina injection, cataract evaluation or post-op. Each one carries its workup time, dilation needs and imaging stations, so staff do not have to remember them.

steps.title: Testing balanced
steps.body: clinIQ checks OCT, visual field and imaging capacity when booking. If too many testing-heavy visits land in one hour, staff see it and spread them across the session. This keeps the imaging room from holding up the physician's next patients and keeps technicians from falling behind.

steps.title: Injection intervals kept
steps.body: Retina patients on anti-VEGF therapy are booked at the interval the physician sets, whether fixed or treat-and-extend. When the interval changes, staff update the series in one step. Each injection's payer approval can be tracked in the [pre-authorization module](/features/pre-auth) alongside the visit.

steps.title: Surgical follow-up booked
steps.body: For cataract patients, pre-op biometry is booked before the surgery date, and post-op visits follow the practice's schedule, such as day one, week one and about a month out. Second-eye surgery can be scheduled once the first eye is cleared, so the episode stays on one timeline.

items.title: Station-aware templates
items.body: Templates include technician workup, dilation, imaging and physician time. The schedule reflects the full visit rather than only the exam, so both technicians and physicians get a realistic day. Templates can be resized later.

items.title: Equipment limits
items.body: OCT, visual field and photography stations are capacity-limited in booking. Testing does not pile up in the same hour, and the physician is not left waiting for results that are still in the queue.

items.title: Subspecialty schedules
items.body: Retina, glaucoma, cornea and comprehensive providers keep their own templates and rules on one system. Practices with several locations keep site-specific rooms and equipment, while traveling physicians see one schedule.

items.title: Recall and interval tracking
items.body: Glaucoma, diabetic eye and injection patients are booked on recall intervals. Staff can see patients who have fallen past their due date and reach out before a missed interval turns into a gap in care.

items.title: Overbooking by visit type
items.body: Short pressure checks and post-op visits can be overbooked in high no-show slots, while long dilated exams cannot. Delays stay bounded, and the clinic still recovers time that no-shows would waste.

faqs.q: How should an ophthalmology practice schedule dilated exams?
faqs.a: Account for the whole visit, not just physician time. Dilated patients need technician workup and time for the drops to take effect, then imaging before the physician sees them. clinIQ uses templates that include each station and spreads testing-heavy visits across the session. Our guide to [ophthalmology diagnostic testing workflow](/blog/ophthalmology-diagnostic-testing-workflow) covers how testing fits in.

faqs.q: How do retina clinics keep anti-VEGF injections on schedule?
faqs.a: Book each patient at the interval the physician sets and update it whenever it changes, whether the plan is fixed dosing or treat-and-extend. clinIQ manages injection visits as a series, flags patients who fall past their due date and lets staff see payer approval status alongside the appointment, so injections are not delayed by missed authorizations.

faqs.q: Can clinIQ schedule cataract pre-op and post-op visits?
faqs.a: Yes. Cataract templates book the evaluation and biometry before surgery and the post-op visits after it, on the practice's standard timeline. Second-eye surgery can be booked once the first eye is cleared. Staff see the whole surgical episode for each patient in one place and can spot a missed post-op visit quickly.

faqs.q: Does clinIQ work with our EHR?
faqs.a: clinIQ can work alongside your EHR scheduling or replace it, depending on your system and preferences. Many eye practices use clinIQ for templates, waitlists, recalls and scheduling rules while appointments sync to the EHR for clinical documentation. Integration keeps both systems consistent without double entry. Setup is scoped during implementation for your EHR.

analytics/mental-health.metaTitle: Mental Health Practice Analytics and Reports
analytics/mental-health.metaDescription: Track no-shows, late cancels, clinician utilization and telehealth versus in-office sessions in your mental health practice. See a demo.
analytics/mental-health.h1: Mental Health Practice Analytics for No-Shows and Clinician Capacity
analytics/mental-health.subtitle: clinIQ shows where sessions are lost and how full each clinician's schedule really is, across in-office and telehealth care.
analytics/mental-health.problemHeading: Empty Hours Are Hard to See
analytics/mental-health.problemStatement: In a mental health practice, a missed session is a lost hour that cannot be backfilled on short notice. No-shows and late cancellations vary by clinician, day, time and whether the session is in office or by video. New clients may come to intake and never return for a second session. Clinicians carry different caseloads and session lengths, and waitlists grow while some calendars have gaps. Without clear reports, directors cannot tell where capacity is lost or which clients need extra outreach.
analytics/mental-health.solutionStatement: clinIQ reports attended, no-show and late-canceled sessions by clinician, day, time slot, modality and lead time. Utilization reports compare booked session hours with each clinician's available hours. Intake reports show how many new clients return for follow-up sessions. Session start and end times show whether sessions start on time, which matters for back-to-back schedules. Directors get a clear picture of capacity and attendance without building spreadsheets by hand.

workflow.h2: How Sessions Turn into Practice Reports
workflow.intro: Each session's status is captured and rolled into attendance and capacity reports.

steps.title: Booking and reminders
steps.body: When a session is booked, clinIQ records the lead time, modality and clinician. Reports later show whether sessions booked far ahead are missed more often, which helps the practice target reminder outreach and decide how far out each clinician's calendar should open.

steps.title: Check-in or video join
steps.body: In-office clients check in and telehealth clients join the video visit. clinIQ logs arrival or join time, so late starts are measured the same way for both modalities. Late arrivals that shorten sessions show up by clinician and time slot.

steps.title: Session start and end
steps.body: Start and end times feed session length and on-time start reports. Directors can see whether back-to-back schedules leave clinicians enough time between clients for notes, and whether certain hours of the day consistently run behind. Patterns that repeat week after week usually point to a template problem, not a clinician problem.

steps.title: Missed session follow-up
steps.body: No-shows and late cancels are reported daily, and clients with repeated missed sessions appear on a follow-up list for outreach. Our post on [behavioral health no-shows](/blog/behavioral-health-no-shows) covers practical outreach approaches that respect client privacy and keep the conversation supportive rather than punitive.

capabilities.h2: Reports Built for Mental Health Practices

items.title: No-show and late cancel rates
items.body: See missed sessions by clinician, weekday, time slot, modality and lead time. The patterns point to where reminders, cancellation policy changes or schedule shifts will recover the most clinical hours each week.

items.title: Clinician utilization
items.body: Compare attended session hours with available hours for each clinician. It shows who has openings for waitlisted clients, who is at capacity and where the practice has room to grow before hiring.

items.title: Intake to second session
items.body: Track how many new clients return after intake, by clinician and referral period. A low return rate points to the first weeks of care as the place to focus engagement and scheduling follow-up.

items.title: Telehealth versus in-office
items.body: Compare attendance, on-time starts and session volume by modality. The practice can then plan office space, video hours and clinician schedules based on real demand. For groups, see our guide to [group therapy scheduling](/blog/group-therapy-scheduling).

faqs.q: What metrics should a mental health practice track?
faqs.a: Start with no-show and late cancel rates, clinician utilization, intake-to-second-session return, on-time session starts and attendance by modality. Time from referral to first appointment matters too when a waitlist exists. clinIQ reports each from booking and session timestamps, broken out by clinician and day, and trends them over time so the practice can see real progress.

faqs.q: How can a therapy practice reduce no-shows?
faqs.a: First find the pattern. clinIQ shows which clinicians, time slots, modalities and lead times have the most missed sessions. Practices then target reminders to high-risk bookings, shorten lead times where possible and follow up quickly with clients who miss. Trend reports show whether those changes worked or need adjusting for specific clinicians or times.

faqs.q: Can clinIQ compare telehealth and in-office attendance?
faqs.a: Yes. Attendance, late starts and session volume are reported by modality, so you can see whether video sessions are kept more or less often than office visits for your clients and clinicians. That helps decide which clients and time slots suit telehealth and how much office space the practice really needs.

faqs.q: Can clinicians see their own numbers?
faqs.a: Yes. Each clinician can view their own utilization, attendance and on-time starts for any period. Directors see the full practice and can compare locations if the group has several offices. Clinicians often use their own reports to adjust session timing and decide when to open more hours for new or waitlisted clients.
